# AGENTS.md

Project: Flint

## What this is
Flint is Claude working as Eric's sport-science, performance, S&C and rehab thought
partner. This repo builds the knowledge base behind that role. It catalogs Eric's
Drive (his own material, TB's Training Info, Landon Evans, courses, papers), routes the
high-value sources into Zotero and the SecondBrain vault, and writes per-discipline
synthesis notes that compare the sources against Eric's own method. It is a side-lane
project, outside the prioritization-slate cap. See `README.md` for the approach and
`docs/PLAN.md` for the checklist.

## Session routine
- Start: run `git pull`, then read docs/STATUS.md before doing anything else.
- End: update docs/STATUS.md (done, next, open questions), commit, and `git push`.
- Never leave uncommitted work at the end of a session.

## Conventions
- Durable notes and decisions go in docs/, committed. Not in chat, not in cloud project docs.
- Documents, data exports, and deliverables live on the primary storage drive (Google Drive 00_Primary_Storage_Drive), not in the repo. Files over 95 MB never go in git.
- `data/` is gitignored except aggregate summaries. Regenerate the file-level manifest with `pwsh scripts/build_manifest.ps1`.
- Codex workers read staged copies in `staging/`, never the Drive root. DexaProject, athlete snapshots, Catapult and PFF exports are never catalogued.
- The ingest review gate has two stages.
  1. Before atomizing, verify the source artifact by an independent route: page order, scanned versus text, transcripts checked against captions.
  2. Before promoting, Codex reviews the staged entries against the staged sources, with instructions to falsify (`staging/review_<source>_codex.md`). Nothing reaches the vault without a GO or a GO AFTER FIXES that has been applied.
- Library entries label every voice. The source author's statements are plain. Eric's judgments get "Eric's review:". The entry writer's own reasoning gets "Inference:". No unlabeled judgments. Every number carries a timestamp or page the reviewer can check, and a claim is only tagged "confirmed in PDF" if that PDF is staged. (Learned from the Harries review, 2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes, mostly for attribution.)
- Writing: plain, direct, no em dashes. Documents use the Baylor design system.

# Issurin 2016 — Benefits and limitations of block-periodized preparation

> **Citation**
> Issurin, V. B. (2016). Benefits and limitations of block periodized training approaches to athletes' preparation: A review. *Sports Medicine, 46*(3), 329–338. https://doi.org/10.1007/s40279-015-0425-5

## Why it was promoted

This review distinguishes concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block models and provides a useful conceptual vocabulary for discussing concentrated workloads and sequencing.

## Research question

What benefits, limitations, and sport-context boundaries are reported for two versions of block-periodized athlete preparation?

## Population and context

- The review emphasizes elite, subelite, and well-trained athletes across endurance, team, combat, dual, jumping, and strength/power settings. [p. 11]
- It also discusses a smaller number of recreational-athlete studies.
- It is a training-theory review, not evidence specific to collegiate American football.

## Study design and methods

- Narrative review contrasting concentrated-unidirectional and multi-targeted block-periodization models.
- The article summarizes prior studies in tables but does not report a systematic search, eligibility process, formal risk-of-bias appraisal, or meta-analysis.
- Consequently, the stated number and direction of supportive studies should be interpreted as an author-curated synthesis rather than a pooled comparative estimate.

## Key findings

- Concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance. [p. 6]
- In an elite-swimmer example, specific strength and anaerobic capacity improved but swimming performance improved in only two of three athletes. [p. 6]
- The author judged the concentrated-unidirectional evidence insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation. [p. 6]
- The review reports support from 28 studies for multi-targeted block programs, but the designs, populations, outcomes, and comparator quality varied. [p. 11]
- The concentrated-unidirectional model was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities. [p. 11]
- Whose model is whose: the concentrated-unidirectional (CU) model is Verkhoshansky's; the multi-targeted model with 28-study support is Issurin's own A-T-R block model. [pp. 6-7, 11] So this review does not dispute Issurin's 2008 book; it repeats the book's critique of traditional planning. The real 2008-2016 difference is on lower-level athletes: the book (p. 33) says they do fine with medium concentration, while this review says "no evidence that amateur athletes have any serious restrictions" with highly concentrated block workloads. [p. 11] (Clarified 2026-09-27 during the Flint review of Issurin's book, checked against the paper pages.)

## Limitations and applicability

- Non-systematic study selection and absent risk-of-bias assessment create a substantial risk of selective emphasis.
- Fitness improvements are not interchangeable with sport-specific performance, availability, or competitive outcomes. [p. 6]
- Training models were not consistently isolated from total volume, intensity, exercise choice, coaching, or athlete history.
- Evidence spans dissimilar sports and training levels; it does not supply validated block durations or effect estimates for collegiate American football.
- The strong conclusion favoring multi-targeted block periodization is the author's synthesis and should not be treated as settled comparative evidence. [p. 11]

## Practitioner interpretation

Use block periodization as a planning hypothesis: concentrate compatible emphases when competition structure and athlete needs justify it, while maintaining the qualities and technical exposure that cannot safely decay. Judge the plan by sport-specific performance, availability, and individual response—not by the periodization label. Compare it prospectively with the program's own prior practice where feasible.

## Evidence map

| Claim | Locator | Evidence type |
|---|---|---|
| Review scope and distinction between two models | p. 4 | narrative framing |
| Concentrated-unidirectional evidence and performance gaps | p. 6 | narrative synthesis |
| Multi-targeted evidence claim and applicability boundaries | p. 11 | narrative synthesis/limitation |

## Related knowledge

- [[periodization]] — annual and phase planning
- [[training-load-concentration]] — sequencing compatible emphases
- [[supertraining--verkhoshansky/framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]: Supertraining 5.3.3's system of successive concentrated blocks; it cites this review's limits for team, combat and swimming preparation as the case against using that system there

Read this whole file before writing anything. It holds the rules the Harries review taught (2026-09-26: 25 of 35 files needed fixes). The review gate will check every rule here.

## Schema

Follow `C:\Users\eric_rash\.claude\skills\ingest-book\SKILL.md` exactly: `_domain.md`, `_book.md` (map and resume checkpoint, updated after EACH chapter or unit), and entries named `<kind>--<kebab-slug>.md` with kind one of principle, framework, case-study, heuristic, claim. Use the frontmatter keys exactly as the skill gives them. The body has **What it is** / **Why it works** / **When to apply** / **When NOT to apply** (mandatory, non-trivial) / **Example** / **Related**.

Style reference, read before writing: `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library\strength-and-conditioning\fundamentals-of-sprinting--moyer\case-study--isometric-sprinter-and-hurdler.md`, plus one principle file in the same folder.

## Voices: label every one

- **The source author's statements are plain text.**
- **Eric's views** (from `docs/method-baseline.md` or his reviews) are prefixed "Eric's baseline:" or "Eric's review:".
- **Your own reasoning, application or synthesis** is prefixed "Inference:".
- **Nothing unlabeled that the author did not say.** The most common failures: a judgment from Eric's review written as if the author said it; a mechanism the author never gave presented as "why it works" (write "The author gives no mechanism. Inference: ..."); an invented example.

## Lessons from the Supertraining Chapter 1 review (2026-09-26: 30 FIX, 1 NO-GO of 41)

- **Keep the source's internal contradictions.** When a book says X on one page and not-X on another, record both with their pages and set `contested`. Never pick one side silently. The NO-GO entry reversed the book's SJ-CMJ strength-deficit rule because the book states it both ways.
- **Name the right voice.** In co-authored books, write "the authors" unless a passage clearly belongs to one author. A passage that names Verkhoshansky in the third person is Siff writing.
- **Keep `proven` rare and scoped.** Scope it to the replicated core (for example, "Hill's force-velocity curve"), never the whole entry, and mark any disputed sentence inside it. Four of eight `proven` ratings were lowered.
- **No mechanism the source does not give.** About a dozen "Why it works" sections supplied physiology the book never states. Label it "Inference:" or leave it out.
- **Do not add "well established" or "modern research shows" without a citation.** Name the paper, or delete the phrase.

## Lessons from the 2026-09-27 review wave (Supertraining Ch2-3, Issurin Ch3, Bondarchuk, Evans, Old Bull)

- **Invented Examples are the most common failure.** 34 of 36 Supertraining Ch2-3a Examples were unlabelled inventions. Use the source's own example where it gives one; otherwise start the Example with "Inference:".
- **"Verified against the page image" means you opened the image.** Four Issurin Ch3 entries claimed it for figures they had misread (Fig 3.7 inverted, a Table 3.7 row swapped). Sparse slides are not "bare diagrams" until you have looked.
- **Name the population and method the source gives.** Bondarchuk's data are 7,000+ native and foreign athletes, questionnaires, r >= 0.349, steroid-free; entries that said "Soviet athletes" were wrong everywhere.
- **Check what a cited paper actually says.** Issurin 2016's critique targets Verkhoshansky's concentrated-unidirectional model, not Issurin's A-T-R; Herzog & Leonard 2000 shows force enhancement, against the book's sentence. When the book misreports a study, record both.
- **No review history in entries.** "Prior version", "corrected from a NO-GO finding" and similar belong in `staging/fixes_*_applied.md`, never in the entry body.
- **Fix logs must match the files.** One fixer log claimed fixes that were not made. Fixers run their own grep checks and paste the output.
- **Section headers use the vault form** `**What it is** —` (with the em dash). Do not add suffixes such as ": mandatory". Em dashes are banned only in titles and body text. Never wrap a `[[wikilink]]` across lines.

## Evidence

- Every number, definition and quote carries a checkable locator: PDF page (and printed page if it differs), or file plus timestamp. Never write "confirmed in PDF" unless you opened that page.
- Never invent a number. Keep ambiguity visible: mark unclear audio or OCR as unclear, and do not harmonize two conflicting numbers from the source; record both with their locators.
- OCR sources (`staging/ocr/*.md`): pages listed as low_confidence in the header must be checked against the page image before any number from them is cited. Use the Read tool on the PDF page, or render it.
- **OCR confidence scores miss the worst errors** (checked 2026-09-27). Zatsiorsky 2e: the OCR interleaves the two columns and the sidebars line by line, so its text is not readable prose; use it only to find content, and read and quote from the page image. *CFTS*: single-column prose that mostly reads in order, but upside-down lines come out as gibberish, some lines are dropped, and figures are scrambled, all at "0 low-confidence pages". For any OCR source, quote only after checking the page image, and read every figure and table from the image.

## Confidence

- Practitioner courses and lectures: ceiling `supported`.
- Books: `proven` only for established, widely replicated physiology or mechanics. Soviet-era or single-lab empirical findings and training prescriptions: `supported` at most. `untested` for single cases and anecdotes. `contested` where another library source or modern evidence disagrees (say which).

## Dedup and converge

Before each entry, grep `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\SecondBrain\Knowledge\library` and the staging library (`C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\staging\library`) for the concept. If it is covered, add a new entry only for a genuinely new angle, and link the existing one in Related. List reciprocal-link suggestions in your final report. Never edit files in the vault or another agent's staging folder.

## Baylor context

Read `C:\Users\eric_rash\Desktop\DEV\Flint\.claude\worktrees\step1-triage\docs\method-baseline.md` (approved). Use it in When to apply, labelled "Eric's baseline:". Department names: Athletic Performance, Athletic Medicine, Applied Performance. Plain style, no em dashes. Use commas, colons and parentheses.

## Scope and output

- Write ONLY into your assigned staging folder. No git, no vault edits.
- Stop at a chapter or unit boundary. It is better to finish fewer chapters well; the `_book.md` checkpoint lets the next batch resume.
- Final reply: entries by kind and by confidence; chapters or units done and pending with page ranges; reciprocal-link suggestions; unclear or contradictory spots in the source; anything you could not read.

Upper panel: all three strength curves (Starting, Explosive, Maximum) fall during block 1 after a small early bump in the two upper curves, rise to a first peak at about months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary), dip again during block 2 (about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross at about months 8-9, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, falls during block 2, then rises to its highest level at about months 9-10 and declines toward month 11. The GPP and Speed curves cross several times and cannot be told apart reliably in the image; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the LDTE: the concentrated block lowers the athlete's state, and the gain appears afterward, so technique and speed work is timed for the period after the block. For concentrated loading in general they state a mechanism at PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370 (checked against the page image): it "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation." The second block can be smaller because it runs "against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle" (PDF p. 394). No data are shown for this model; Fig 6.39 is a schematic credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6), and saw the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. American football is a team sport. Other limits: the model is drawn for "highly qualified athletes" (the concentrated method "was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes," PDF p. 381); the block rectangles are not literal ("The use of rectangular blocks should not create the impression that the concentrated loads are applied suddenly at peak intensity," PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380); and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar (PDF p. 391). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: that rule fits the model's phase IV, where the strength block is over, but the model gives no in-season strength dose, and the baseline's game week ("lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game," line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)) is a microcycle rule the annual model does not address.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors give the model, not a worked year (Fig 6.39, PDF p. 395). Inference: for a jumper with indoor and outdoor seasons, block 1 would sit in the first three months of autumn preparation with the jumps, weights and depth-jump sequence inside it, the indoor season would fall about month 5, block 2 would run about months 6-7 at less volume and more intensity, and the main outdoor competitions would fall in months 9-11.
    32	
    33	**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[heuristic--follow-a-concentrated-block-with-moderate-volume-explosive-work]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]

    14	# Tri-Cyclic Model for Individual and One-on-One Sports: Three Mesocycles for SPP, Technical Mastery and Competition Readiness, Each With Its Own Strength Block
    15	
    16	**What it is** — 6.14.4 (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image; Fig 6.42 on PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387, checked against the image): "The tri-cyclic model is intended primarily for individual and one-on-one sports (Fig 6.42). It comprises three mesocycles, with preparatory and competitive micro-stages. The first stage is oriented chiefly towards special physical preparation; the second, to perfecting technical mastery, and the third, to readiness for the major competitions." The third stage "can be increased by shortening the duration of the second stage," and "In certain cases a bi-cyclic model of training can be employed with this group of sports."
    17	- **Athlete-state model:** maximum aerobic productivity in the second stage, then some decrease; "Maximum strength rises uniformly, while strength-endurance accelerates more during the third stage. Explosive strength reaches a maximum at the beginning of the second and at the end of the third stages."
    18	- **Three strength blocks:** the first "to develop maximum and explosive strength; the second, to develop strength-endurance; the third, chiefly to increase explosive strength and create conditions for exploiting the LDTE of the strength loading during the fundamental competition phase."
    19	- **Energy-system pairing:** "The first and third blocks of strength work are executed in combination with special work in the mixed (aerobic-anaerobic) zone of energy production, while the second is combined with work in the anaerobic (ATP-CP and anaerobic-glycolytic) zone. The fundamental volume of speed and technical-tactical preparation is executed against a background of the LDTE elicited by the blocks of strength work."
    20	- **Fig 6.42, read by eye:** phases I about months 1-4, II about months 5-8, III about months 9-11. Block 1 about months 1-3 (tallest), block 2 about months 5-6, block 3 about months 9-10 (shortest). The labels at the right edge of the upper panel read, top to bottom, Explosive strength, Anaerobic capacity, Aerobic capacity, Strength-endurance, with Maximum strength lowest and rising nearly linearly. Shorter mesocycles of this kind "should not shift achieving the objective of optimal enhancement of the current adaptation reserves (CAR) to the next stage" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).
    21	
    22	**Why it works** — The authors give the structure, not a mechanism beyond the LDTE of each strength block. No data are shown; the figure is credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
    23	
    24	**When to apply** — Individual and combat sports with three main competition periods, such as the boxing and swimming examples the authors cite for tri-cyclic forms (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376), and team sports where "tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar" (PDF p. 387). Eric's baseline: "The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 188, Inferred (transcript)).     14	# Two Large Mesocycles a Year, the Second Peaking Higher: the Authors Question Monocyclic Periodisation but Keep It for Long-Duration Endurance
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "Research shows that it is appropriate to use two large mesocycles in the annual cycle to promote supercompensation of the current adaptation reserves (Figure 6.34). In this case, the athlete's state displays two large peaks, with the second one producing the higher special work-capacity (i.e. fitness state). This further corroborates the value of this form of bi-cyclic organisation of annual preparation which was empirically worked out and applied successfully long ago in several sports" (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376, checked against the page image). "Consequently, unquestioning adherence to monocyclic periodisation in a number of sports is not justified, and it is advisable that coaches re-examine this tradition carefully." Bi-cyclic periodisation may also suit sports that traditionally use monocyclic forms (skiing, Ogoltsov, 1979; middle-distance running, Turin, 1980; Sirenko, 1980) or tri-cyclic forms (boxing, Nikiforov & Viktorov, 1978; swimming, Vaitsekhovsky, 1981). "In a number of team sports and one-on-one events, tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar, whereas in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387).
    17	
    18	The first primary aim of programming (6.13) repeats it: "It is appropriate to fit at least two large mesocycles into the annual cycle, even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period and use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389 / printed p. 378, checked against the page image). The practical principles add: "the optimal period for enhancing the current adaptation reserves is about 20 weeks for the most efficient loading of highly qualified athletes," and "the first mesocycle should always be considered as the foundation for the second" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image).
    19	
    20	Fig 6.34 (PDF p. 387, read from the image, no numeric scale): two shaded strength-loading waves, V1 and V2. The fitness-state curve dips during V1, rises to a peak between the waves, dips again during V2, and then climbs to a level above the first peak at the right edge.
    21	
    22	**Contested inside the book.** Aim 1 says "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389), but the same chapter says "in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387) and gives a monocyclic model for them with "one competitive stage" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385). The authors partly reconcile this: the monocyclic endurance model still contains "a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training" with two strength blocks (PDF p. 396). See [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]].
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is supercompensation of the "current adaptation reserves" and the claim that the second mesocycle builds on the first. They cite no data for the second peak being higher beyond "research shows" and long empirical use.
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Sports with two main competition periods, or one long one where an intermediate peak is useful. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: if the winter-spring and summer off-season phases are treated as the two large mesocycles, the authors' rule that the second builds on the first and peaks higher fits a fall season with a November priority window; the authors do not discuss football.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — **Also contested by Issurin** on the length and number of training units. Issurin's training stage "should be about two months," and the number of stages "usually varies from four to seven" a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], Block Periodization PDF pp. 38-40), against the authors' two large mesocycles of usually 3-5 months (PDF p. 387) and "about 20 weeks" to enhance the adaptation reserves (PDF p. 400). Bompa's cycle types as taught by Evans reserve the bicycle for "ADVANCED OR ELITE ATHLETES" and the monocycle for novice and junior athletes ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]); the authors' models are likewise for qualified athletes. Long-duration endurance sports stay monocyclic in the authors' own scheme.

    30	**Example** — The authors' illustration is Fig 6.34 and the bi-cyclic models of 6.14.1 and 6.14.2 ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Inference: a middle-distance runner with an indoor season in winter and the main outdoor championship in late summer runs two large mesocycles of about four to five months each, the first ending at the indoor meets.

    13	
    14	# Complex (Concurrent) Training Suits Beginners and Average Athletes; for Highly Qualified Athletes the Authors Favour Single-Emphasis Workouts, Microcycles and Stages
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).
    17	
    18	Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
    19	- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
    20	- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
    21	- **Three deficiencies for highly qualified athletes.** (1) Their very high special preparedness needs "strong and relatively prolonged training influences of appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this." (2) "Complex training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing highly specific physical preparedness." (3) "Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control" (PDF p. 380). These deficiencies "are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification."
    22	- **Evidence for single-emphasis units.** Single-emphasis workouts make adaptation "more marked" (Handelsman & Stetsenko, 1980); sessions devoted solely to technique are "very effective in improving technical skill" (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977); single-ability sessions "exert a more profound effect on special preparedness" than multi-objective sessions (five studies cited); single-emphasis microcycles "powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980)" and strength-emphasis microcycles "significantly raise the special physical preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981)" (PDF p. 381).
    23	- **The resolution: complexity over time.** "*The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) method as the most general principle of training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements of conditioning highly qualified athletes.* Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not its contents and structure at a given instant" (italics in the original; PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373). Complex preparation "is limited as a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development."
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are the three deficiencies above: too weak a stimulus in any one direction, too little specificity, and fatigue that degrades technical control. Their stated mechanism for the alternative is "the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary emphasis" (PDF p. 384). No effect sizes are given for any cited study.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Issurin's multi-targeted block model trains a minimal number of targets per block, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), and the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records the multi-targeted model's 28-study support against insufficient evidence for the concentrated-unidirectional model in team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).

15	    14	# Annual Model for Explosive-Strength Sports: Two Mesocycles, Two Concentrated Strength Blocks, the Second Smaller in Volume and Higher in Intensity
16	    15	
17	    16	**What it is** — The authors' prescriptive model for sports "requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383; Fig 6.39 on PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384; both pages checked against the page images, the figure also at 300 dpi). The text gives these rules:
18	    17	1. **Bi-cyclic structure.** "This model involves bi-cyclic periodisation of training and includes two mesocycles aimed at optimally developing the body's current adaptation reserves and achieving the planned level of special-strength preparedness at the most important competitions." The fitness model tracks "absolute, explosive and starting strength indicators, the highest values of which are achieved at the end of each mesocycle" (PDF p. 394).
19	    18	2. **Strength blocks against a background of speed and technique.** "The organisation of loading provides for exploiting the LDTE of the block of strength work in each mesocycle against a background of the fundamental speed and technical training. The basic principle is block loading with means of different primary emphasis." Technique is "not excluded during the strength loading block. However, such work is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links (see 2.1.2), as well as the rhythmic patterns of individual phases" (PDF p. 394). LDTE is the book's long-term delayed training effect of concentrated strength loading.
20	    19	3. **Second block: less volume, more intensity.** "The second strength block imposes a smaller volume, although the general loading intensity is higher than in the first block. Since the second block is executed against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle, the LDTE will be preserved during the second competitive stage. It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work, which can be used exclusively for preparing the neuromuscular system before the subsequent training that emphasizes technique or competitive readiness" (PDF p. 394).
21	    20	4. **Block contents.** The blocks follow "the principle of preserving the training potential of the loading by means of the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3)" (PDF p. 394). The section just before 6.14.1 shows what a speed-strength block holds: "Jumping > Weights exercises > Plyometrics," "not sharply separated by time intervals, but substituted continuously for one another, ensuring that intensity and functional indicators are monitored carefully to avoid overtraining" (PDF p. 394; Fig 6.38, Verkhoshansky 1977). In Fig 6.38 the three overlapping volume waves are A jumps (early, small), B weights exercises (middle, the largest) and C plyometric depth jumps (late, small); read from the image, no numeric axis.
22	    21	5. **GPP.** "Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised loading... The largest relative volume of GPP means occurs during the competitive periods" (PDF p. 394). See [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]].
23	    22	
24	    23	**Fig 6.39, read from the image (all month values "about"; no vertical scale).** The time axis runs 11 months (the 6.14 conventions: "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period," PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379). Phases: I (1st preparation) about months 1-4, II (1st competition) about month 5, III (2nd preparation) about months 6-8, IV (2nd competition) about months 9-11. The phase boundaries and dashed lines do not fall exactly on the month ticks (phase I ends late in month 4; phase III ends during month 8). Block 1 is a tall shaded rectangle over about months 1-3; block 2 is a shorter rectangle over about months 6-7, roughly two thirds of block 1's height, matching the text's "smaller volume." Upper panel: all three strength curves (Starting, Explosive, Maximum) fall during block 1 after a small early bump in the two upper curves, rise to a first peak at about months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary), dip again during block 2 (about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross at about months 8-9, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, falls during block 2, then rises to its highest level at about months 9-10 and declines toward month 11. The GPP and Speed curves cross several times and cannot be told apart reliably in the image; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.
25	    24	
26	    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the LDTE: the concentrated block lowers the athlete's state, and the gain appears afterward, so technique and speed work is timed for the period after the block. For concentrated loading in general they state a mechanism at PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370 (checked against the page image): it "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation." The second block can be smaller because it runs "against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle" (PDF p. 394). No data are shown for this model; Fig 6.39 is a schematic credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
27	    26	
28	    27	**When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.
29	    28	
30	    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6), and saw the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. American football is a team sport. Other limits: the model is drawn for "highly qualified athletes" (the concentrated method "was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes," PDF p. 381); the block rectangles are not literal ("The use of rectangular blocks should not create the impression that the concentrated loads are applied suddenly at peak intensity," PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380); and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar (PDF p. 391). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: that rule fits the model's phase IV, where the strength block is over, but the model gives no in-season strength dose, and the baseline's game week ("lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game," line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)) is a microcycle rule the annual model does not address.
31	    30	
32	    31	**Example** — The authors give the model, not a worked year (Fig 6.39, PDF p. 395). Inference: for a jumper with indoor and outdoor seasons, block 1 would sit in the first three months of autumn preparation with the jumps, weights and depth-jump sequence inside it, the indoor season would fall about month 5, block 2 would run about months 6-7 at less volume and more intensity, and the main outdoor competitions would fall in months 9-11.
33	    32	
34	    33	**Related** — [[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[heuristic--sequence-jumps-then-barbell-then-depth-jumps-across-stages]], [[heuristic--allow-restoration-after-a-concentrated-block-before-the-next]], [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[heuristic--follow-a-concentrated-block-with-moderate-volume-explosive-work]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]

49	    14	# Tri-Cyclic Model for Individual and One-on-One Sports: Three Mesocycles for SPP, Technical Mastery and Competition Readiness, Each With Its Own Strength Block
50	    15	
51	    16	**What it is** — 6.14.4 (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image; Fig 6.42 on PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387, checked against the image): "The tri-cyclic model is intended primarily for individual and one-on-one sports (Fig 6.42). It comprises three mesocycles, with preparatory and competitive micro-stages. The first stage is oriented chiefly towards special physical preparation; the second, to perfecting technical mastery, and the third, to readiness for the major competitions." The third stage "can be increased by shortening the duration of the second stage," and "In certain cases a bi-cyclic model of training can be employed with this group of sports."
52	    17	- **Athlete-state model:** maximum aerobic productivity in the second stage, then some decrease; "Maximum strength rises uniformly, while strength-endurance accelerates more during the third stage. Explosive strength reaches a maximum at the beginning of the second and at the end of the third stages."
53	    18	- **Three strength blocks:** the first "to develop maximum and explosive strength; the second, to develop strength-endurance; the third, chiefly to increase explosive strength and create conditions for exploiting the LDTE of the strength loading during the fundamental competition phase."
54	    19	- **Energy-system pairing:** "The first and third blocks of strength work are executed in combination with special work in the mixed (aerobic-anaerobic) zone of energy production, while the second is combined with work in the anaerobic (ATP-CP and anaerobic-glycolytic) zone. The fundamental volume of speed and technical-tactical preparation is executed against a background of the LDTE elicited by the blocks of strength work."
55	    20	- **Fig 6.42, read by eye:** phases I about months 1-4, II about months 5-8, III about months 9-11. Block 1 about months 1-3 (tallest), block 2 about months 5-6, block 3 about months 9-10 (shortest). The labels at the right edge of the upper panel read, top to bottom, Explosive strength, Anaerobic capacity, Aerobic capacity, Strength-endurance, with Maximum strength lowest and rising nearly linearly. Shorter mesocycles of this kind "should not shift achieving the objective of optimal enhancement of the current adaptation reserves (CAR) to the next stage" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).
56	    21	
57	    22	**Why it works** — The authors give the structure, not a mechanism beyond the LDTE of each strength block. No data are shown; the figure is credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
58	    23	
59	    24	**When to apply** — Individual and combat sports with three main competition periods, such as the boxing and swimming examples the authors cite for tri-cyclic forms (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376), and team sports where "tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar" (PDF p. 387). Eric's baseline: "The head coach's system of play and roster identity (e.g., a "home run hitters" lineup vs. a "steal bases" lineup) is treated as a direct input into whether a team's programming leans toward maximal strength or toward speed/power emphasis" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 188, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the model's block contents (maximum, endurance, explosive) are the kind of lever that input would set.
60	    25	
61	    26	**When NOT to apply** — **Issurin 2016 challenge (combat sports).** The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports improved some fitness measures without reported effects on practice or competitive performance, and that Issurin judged the evidence insufficient for broad use in "high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6; [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]). This entry keeps `supported` because the tri-cyclic layout itself is not what Issurin challenges; the challenge is to the concentrated blocks inside it, recorded on [[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]]. The model assumes three distinct competition peaks; it is not a template for a weekly-competition season.
62	    27	
63	    28	**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a wrestler with a winter national championship, a spring continental event and a late-summer world championship runs a maximum-strength block in autumn, a strength-endurance block in late winter with anaerobic work, and a short explosive block before the summer peak.
64	    29	
65	    30	**Related** — [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]

80	    14	# Two Large Mesocycles a Year, the Second Peaking Higher: the Authors Question Monocyclic Periodisation but Keep It for Long-Duration Endurance
81	    15	
82	    16	**What it is** — "Research shows that it is appropriate to use two large mesocycles in the annual cycle to promote supercompensation of the current adaptation reserves (Figure 6.34). In this case, the athlete's state displays two large peaks, with the second one producing the higher special work-capacity (i.e. fitness state). This further corroborates the value of this form of bi-cyclic organisation of annual preparation which was empirically worked out and applied successfully long ago in several sports" (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376, checked against the page image). "Consequently, unquestioning adherence to monocyclic periodisation in a number of sports is not justified, and it is advisable that coaches re-examine this tradition carefully." Bi-cyclic periodisation may also suit sports that traditionally use monocyclic forms (skiing, Ogoltsov, 1979; middle-distance running, Turin, 1980; Sirenko, 1980) or tri-cyclic forms (boxing, Nikiforov & Viktorov, 1978; swimming, Vaitsekhovsky, 1981). "In a number of team sports and one-on-one events, tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar, whereas in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387).
83	    17	
84	    18	The first primary aim of programming (6.13) repeats it: "It is appropriate to fit at least two large mesocycles into the annual cycle, even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period and use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389 / printed p. 378, checked against the page image). The practical principles add: "the optimal period for enhancing the current adaptation reserves is about 20 weeks for the most efficient loading of highly qualified athletes," and "the first mesocycle should always be considered as the foundation for the second" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image).
85	    19	
86	    20	Fig 6.34 (PDF p. 387, read from the image, no numeric scale): two shaded strength-loading waves, V1 and V2. The fitness-state curve dips during V1, rises to a peak between the waves, dips again during V2, and then climbs to a level above the first peak at the right edge.
87	    21	
88	    22	**Contested inside the book.** Aim 1 says "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389), but the same chapter says "in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387) and gives a monocyclic model for them with "one competitive stage" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385). The authors partly reconcile this: the monocyclic endurance model still contains "a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training" with two strength blocks (PDF p. 396). See [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]].
89	    23	
90	    24	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is supercompensation of the "current adaptation reserves" and the claim that the second mesocycle builds on the first. They cite no data for the second peak being higher beyond "research shows" and long empirical use.
91	    25	
92	    26	**When to apply** — Sports with two main competition periods, or one long one where an intermediate peak is useful. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: if the winter-spring and summer off-season phases are treated as the two large mesocycles, the authors' rule that the second builds on the first and peaks higher fits a fall season with a November priority window; the authors do not discuss football.
93	    27	
94	    28	**When NOT to apply** — **Also contested by Issurin** on the length and number of training units. Issurin's training stage "should be about two months," and the number of stages "usually varies from four to seven" a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], Block Periodization PDF pp. 38-40), against the authors' two large mesocycles of usually 3-5 months (PDF p. 387) and "about 20 weeks" to enhance the adaptation reserves (PDF p. 400). Bompa's cycle types as taught by Evans reserve the bicycle for "ADVANCED OR ELITE ATHLETES" and the monocycle for novice and junior athletes ([[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]); the authors' models are likewise for qualified athletes. Long-duration endurance sports stay monocyclic in the authors' own scheme.
95	    29	
96	    30	**Example** — The authors' illustration is Fig 6.34 and the bi-cyclic models of 6.14.1 and 6.14.2 ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Inference: a middle-distance runner with an indoor season in winter and the main outdoor championship in late summer runs two large mesocycles of about four to five months each, the first ending at the indoor meets.
97	    31	
98	    32	**Related** — [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]], [[heuristic--set-mesocycle-boundaries-by-main-competition-dates]], [[framework--tricyclic-annual-model-for-individual-and-one-on-one-sports]], [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]], [[elite-sports-performance--evans/framework--bompa-annual-plan-cycle-types]]

100	     1	---
101	     2	type: library-entry

112	    13	
113	    14	# Complex (Concurrent) Training Suits Beginners and Average Athletes; for Highly Qualified Athletes the Authors Favour Single-Emphasis Workouts, Microcycles and Stages
114	    15	
115	    16	**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).
116	    17	
117	    18	Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
118	    19	- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
119	    20	- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
120	    21	- **Three deficiencies for highly qualified athletes.** (1) Their very high special preparedness needs "strong and relatively prolonged training influences of appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this." (2) "Complex training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing highly specific physical preparedness." (3) "Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control" (PDF p. 380). These deficiencies "are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification."
121	    22	- **Evidence for single-emphasis units.** Single-emphasis workouts make adaptation "more marked" (Handelsman & Stetsenko, 1980); sessions devoted solely to technique are "very effective in improving technical skill" (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977); single-ability sessions "exert a more profound effect on special preparedness" than multi-objective sessions (five studies cited); single-emphasis microcycles "powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980)" and strength-emphasis microcycles "significantly raise the special physical preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981)" (PDF p. 381).
122	    23	- **The resolution: complexity over time.** "*The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) method as the most general principle of training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements of conditioning highly qualified athletes.* Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not its contents and structure at a given instant" (italics in the original; PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373). Complex preparation "is limited as a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development."
123	    24	
124	    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are the three deficiencies above: too weak a stimulus in any one direction, too little specificity, and fatigue that degrades technical control. Their stated mechanism for the alternative is "the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary emphasis" (PDF p. 384). No effect sizes are given for any cited study.
125	    26	
126	    27	**When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.
127	    28	
128	    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Issurin's multi-targeted block model trains a minimal number of targets per block, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), and the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records the multi-targeted model's 28-study support against insufficient evidence for the concentrated-unidirectional model in team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.
129	    30	
130	    31	**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).
131	    32	
132	    33	**Related** — [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]], [[framework--sequential-and-concurrent-variants-of-systematic-means]], [[claim--concentrated-strength-loading-limited-period-qualified-athletes-and-volume-saving]], [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]], [[claim--strength-and-speed-training-response-shifts-with-training-age]], [[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]], [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]

=================== framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports
     1	---

     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.14.1"
     7	topic: explosive strength annual model
     8	category: [periodization, annual-plan, concentrated-loading, explosive-strength, bi-cyclic, speed-strength]
     9	confidence: contested

    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Annual Model for Explosive-Strength Sports: Two Mesocycles, Two Concentrated Strength Blocks, the Second Smaller in Volume and Higher in Intensity
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors' prescriptive model for sports "requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383; Fig 6.39 on PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384; both pages checked against the page images, the figure also at 300 dpi). The text gives these rules:
    17	1. **Bi-cyclic structure.** "This model involves bi-cyclic periodisation of training and includes two mesocycles aimed at optimally developing the body's current adaptation reserves and achieving the planned level of special-strength preparedness at the most important competitions." The fitness model tracks "absolute, explosive and starting strength indicators, the highest values of which are achieved at the end of each mesocycle" (PDF p. 394).
    18	2. **Strength blocks against a background of speed and technique.** "The organisation of loading provides for exploiting the LDTE of the block of strength work in each mesocycle against a background of the fundamental speed and technical training. The basic principle is block loading with means of different primary emphasis." Technique is "not excluded during the strength loading block. However, such work is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links (see 2.1.2), as well as the rhythmic patterns of individual phases" (PDF p. 394). LDTE is the book's long-term delayed training effect of concentrated strength loading.
    19	3. **Second block: less volume, more intensity.** "The second strength block imposes a smaller volume, although the general loading intensity is higher than in the first block. Since the second block is executed against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle, the LDTE will be preserved during the second competitive stage. It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work, which can be used exclusively for preparing the neuromuscular system before the subsequent training that emphasizes technique or competitive readiness" (PDF p. 394).
    20	4. **Block contents.** The blocks follow "the principle of preserving the training potential of the loading by means of the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3)" (PDF p. 394). The section just before 6.14.1 shows what a speed-strength block holds: "Jumping > Weights exercises > Plyometrics," "not sharply separated by time intervals, but substituted continuously for one another, ensuring that intensity and functional indicators are monitored carefully to avoid overtraining" (PDF p. 394; Fig 6.38, Verkhoshansky 1977). In Fig 6.38 the three overlapping volume waves are A jumps (early, small), B weights exercises (middle, the largest) and C plyometric depth jumps (late, small); read from the image, no numeric axis.
    21	5. **GPP.** "Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised loading... The largest relative volume of GPP means occurs during the competitive periods" (PDF p. 394). See [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]].
    22	
    23	**Fig 6.39, read from the image (all month values "about"; no vertical scale).** The time axis runs 11 months (the 6.14 conventions: "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period," PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379). Phases: I (1st preparation) about months 1-4, II (1st competition) about month 5, III (2nd preparation) about months 6-8, IV (2nd competition) about months 9-11. The phase boundaries and dashed lines do not fall exactly on the month ticks (phase I ends late in month 4; phase III ends during month 8). Block 1 is a tall shaded rectangle over about months 1-3; block 2 is a shorter rectangle over about months 6-7, roughly two thirds of block 1's height, matching the text's "smaller volume." Upper panel: all three strength curves (Starting, Explosive, Maximum) fall during block 1 after a small early bump in the two upper curves, rise to a first peak at about months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary), dip again during block 2 (about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross at about months 8-9, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, falls during block 2, then rises to its highest level at about months 9-10 and declines toward month 11. The GPP and Speed curves cross several times and cannot be told apart reliably in the image; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the LDTE: the concentrated block lowers the athlete's state, and the gain appears afterward, so technique and speed work is timed for the period after the block. For concentrated loading in general they state a mechanism at PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370 (checked against the page image): it "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation." The second block can be smaller because it runs "against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle" (PDF p. 394). No data are shown for this model; Fig 6.39 is a schematic credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image).     14	# Two Large Mesocycles a Year, the Second Peaking Higher: the Authors Question Monocyclic Periodisation but Keep It for Long-Duration Endurance
    15	
    16	**What it is** — "Research shows that it is appropriate to use two large mesocycles in the annual cycle to promote supercompensation of the current adaptation reserves (Figure 6.34). In this case, the athlete's state displays two large peaks, with the second one producing the higher special work-capacity (i.e. fitness state). This further corroborates the value of this form of bi-cyclic organisation of annual preparation which was empirically worked out and applied successfully long ago in several sports" (PDF p. 387 / printed p. 376, checked against the page image). "Consequently, unquestioning adherence to monocyclic periodisation in a number of sports is not justified, and it is advisable that coaches re-examine this tradition carefully." Bi-cyclic periodisation may also suit sports that traditionally use monocyclic forms (skiing, Ogoltsov, 1979; middle-distance running, Turin, 1980; Sirenko, 1980) or tri-cyclic forms (boxing, Nikiforov & Viktorov, 1978; swimming, Vaitsekhovsky, 1981). "In a number of team sports and one-on-one events, tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar, whereas in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended" (PDF p. 387).
    17	
    18	The first primary aim of programming (6.13) repeats it: "It is appropriate to fit at least two large mesocycles into the annual cycle, even in sports which traditionally have one main competitive period and use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389 / printed p. 378, checked against the page image). The practical principles add: "the optimal period for enhancing the current adaptation reserves is about 20 weeks for the most efficient loading of highly qualified athletes," and "the first mesocycle should always be considered as the foundation for the second" (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389, checked against the page image).
    19	
    20	Fig 6.34 (PDF p. 387, read from the image, no numeric scale): two shaded strength-loading waves, V1 and V2. The fitness-state curve dips during V1, rises to a peak between the waves, dips again during V2, and then climbs to a level above the first peak at the right edge.

    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is supercompensation of the "current adaptation reserves" and the claim that the second mesocycle builds on the first. They cite no data for the second peak being higher beyond "research shows" and long empirical use.
