    13	
    14	# Complex (Concurrent) Training Suits Beginners and Average Athletes; for Highly Qualified Athletes the Authors Favour Single-Emphasis Workouts, Microcycles and Stages
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Using complex means requires knowing how the means interact through "the acute and delayed after-effects of each" (PDF p. 379).
    17	
    18	Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):
    19	- **The supporting research is old and used weak athletes.** The early studies (Krestovnikov, 1951; Letunov et al., 1954; Zimkin, 1956; Korobkov et al, 1960; Matveyev, 1970) found complex loading gave balanced fitness and better strength, speed and endurance than unidirectional work. The authors call these concepts "indisputable in principle," but "the research supporting these ideas was done many years ago and utilised athletes of low qualification... under modern conditions this loading would be applicable only to beginners or athletes of average qualification" (PDF p. 380).
    20	- **Verkhoshansky's verdict.** "According to Verkhoshansky (1977), there generally appears to be little advantage for high-level athletes to utilise the complex system of training, although one should not dismiss their possible value at different stages of training with certain individuals in specific cases" (PDF p. 380).
    21	- **Three deficiencies for highly qualified athletes.** (1) Their very high special preparedness needs "strong and relatively prolonged training influences of appropriate emphasis. Complex training does not achieve this." (2) "Complex training, with its multifaceted influence on the body, cannot create the conditions necessary for producing highly specific physical preparedness." (3) "Extensive complex loading to simultaneously perfect sport technique and special physical preparedness inevitably leads to general fatigue and deterioration of this control" (PDF p. 380). These deficiencies "are not as noticeable in athletes of average qualification."
    22	- **Evidence for single-emphasis units.** Single-emphasis workouts make adaptation "more marked" (Handelsman & Stetsenko, 1980); sessions devoted solely to technique are "very effective in improving technical skill" (Struchkov, 1980; Mironenko, 1981; Petrovsky, 1977); single-ability sessions "exert a more profound effect on special preparedness" than multi-objective sessions (five studies cited); single-emphasis microcycles "powerfully stimulate the trainability of swimmers (Kudelin, 1980)" and strength-emphasis microcycles "significantly raise the special physical preparedness of track-and-field jumpers (Mironenko, 1981)" (PDF p. 381).
    23	- **The resolution: complexity over time.** "*The conjugate sequence system does not reject the complex (concurrent) method as the most general principle of training, but only extends it so that it meets the requirements of conditioning highly qualified athletes.* Complexity should be understood in terms of its evolution over time, not its contents and structure at a given instant" (italics in the original; PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373). Complex preparation "is limited as a general principle for training all athletes at all stages of development."
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reasons are the three deficiencies above: too weak a stimulus in any one direction, too little specificity, and fatigue that degrades technical control. Their stated mechanism for the alternative is "the summation of positive, accumulated after-effects of preceding loading of different primary emphasis" (PDF p. 384). No effect sizes are given for any cited study.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Deciding whether a well-trained athlete's week should mix every quality in each session or give whole sessions and whole weeks to one emphasis. Eric's baseline: "Training-compatibility is an explicit constraint on programming: incompatible qualities (e.g., maximal strength work and glycolytic-capacity work) are not both targeted at full intensity in the same block" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 182, Inferred (transcript + slides)). Inference: the baseline and the authors agree that not everything is trained hard at once; the baseline still trains other qualities "at a retention dose," closer to Issurin's multi-targeted blocks than to a single emphasis.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Issurin's multi-targeted block model trains a minimal number of targets per block, not one ([[block-periodization--issurin/principle--concentration-of-training-workloads]]), and the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records the multi-targeted model's 28-study support against insufficient evidence for the concentrated-unidirectional model in team, combat and swimming preparation ([[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]], pp. 6-7, 11). Inside the book there is a caveat a few pages later: a swimming week built from single-emphasis workouts of different kinds still "typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation" and "fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388 / printed pp. 376-377; see [[case-study--unidirectional-weekly-microcycles-swimming-and-speed-strength]]). So single-emphasis workouts alone are not enough; the authors want the emphasis held across a microcycle or stage. Unidirectional loading "is effective only if it forms part of a complex of several means of a single primary emphasis involving a variety of methods" (PDF p. 381). The argument is for highly qualified athletes; for beginners the authors keep complex training.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors' own example of a complex unit: a workout of "resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting," or a week using those means on different days (PDF p. 379). Their single-emphasis examples are the swimmer and jumper microcycles of Kudelin (1980) and Mironenko (1981) (PDF p. 381).

forms and skills of training prescribed for all the microcycies. The duration of the large mesocycle can vary 
(usually 3-5 months), since its calculation depends on the competition calendar and especially on the dates of the 
most important competitions.
Research shows that it is appropriate to use two large mesocycles in the annual cycle to promote 
supercompensation of the current adaptation reserves (Figure 6.34). In this case, the athlete's state displays two 
large peaks, with the second one producing the higher special work-capacity (i.e. fitness state). This further 
corroborates the value of this form of bi-cyclic organisation of annual preparation which was empirically worked 
out and applied successfully long ago in several sports.
Consequently, unquestioning adherence to monocyclic periodisation in a number of sports is not justified, 
and it is advisable that coaches re-examine this tradition carefully. Bi-cyclic periodisation may also be applied in 
several different types of sport which traditionally employ other forms of periodisation, in particular monocyclic 
forms in skiing (Ogoltsov, 1979) and middle-distancc running (Turin, 1980; Sirenko, 1980), as well as tri-cyclical 
forms in boxing (Nikiforov & Viktorov, 1978) and swimming (Vaitsekhovsky, 1981). In a number of team sports 
and one-on-one events, tri-cyclic periodisation may have to be used, as dictated by the competition calendar, 
whereas in long-duration endurance sports, monocyclic periodisation is usually recommended.

relevant now to examine the microcycle more carefully.

complicates the structuring the microcycle. In this respect, all traditional schemes of constructing a microcycle 
with complex training to achieve several simultaneous training objectives and increase specific work capacity at 
the beginning of a new microcycle do not satisfy these requirements. It is necessary to seek new forms of 
constructing microcycies which permit the use of high volumes of loading, including unidirectional regimes. It is 
important to note that microcycies are the basic units of training construction, whose function is to utilise those 
parts of the volume which help them to comply with the objectives and general strategy of the mesocycle.
It is relevant now to examine the currently scant experimental findings which suggest ways of solving these 
problems. It has been established that large unidirectional loading sharply reduces the capability of displaying 
those qualities and abilities which facilitate the effective and safe execution of training programmes. At the same 
time, athletes who exhibit a high work capacity generally achieve it by means of other training systems 
(Monogarov& Platonov, 1975; Fedorova et al, 1975; Chepclyev, 1980; Platonov, 1980).

needed by highly qualified swimmers after high volume unidirectional workouts. The scheme was intended to 
achieve a generally high volume of loading using a systematic combination of workouts of different magnitude 
and emphasis which took into account the duration of the accompanying restoration processes.

differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading and respond to them with

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Weekly Microcycles for Swimmers and Speed-Strength Athletes: a Mixed Week of Single-Emphasis Workouts Gave Volume but No Clear Supercompensation; Single-Emphasis Weeks Showed 72-Hour Restoration Patterns
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors present three weekly microcycles (PDF pp. 387-389 / printed pp. 376-378; all pages and figures checked against the page images). They call the microcycle "the basic units of training construction" and say the traditional complex microcycle cannot carry the volume a large mesocycle needs (PDF p. 387).
    17	
    18	1. **A mixed week for highly qualified swimmers (Fig 6.35, PDF p. 388).** The week was built from the restoration time each workout type needs. The bars read: day 1 aerobic, day 2 speed, day 3 complex (lower bar), day 4 anaerobic, day 5 aerobic, day 6 complex (lower bar), day 7 empty. The "trend of restoration" curve, which "combines the separate effects on restoration for the aerobic, anaerobic and speed components," wavers around a flat line with its deepest dip around days 2-3. The authors' verdict: "despite the uni-directional character of individual workouts, the microcycle as the whole typifies the complex (multi-faceted) form of training organisation. The body cannot simultaneously differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading... this form of microcycle construction enables one to achieve a large volume of loading, but the absence of any marked supercompensation (as revealed by the trend of restoration curve) shows that it fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388).
    19	2. **Single-emphasis swimming weeks (Fig 6.36, PDF p. 388; caption credits "Kubelin, 1980," the text and PDF p. 381 spell it "Kudelin").** Each week has three aerobic (or three anaerobic) workouts on days 1, 3 and 6, with speed-strength, complex and speed-endurance workouts on days 2, 4 and 5, and day 7 empty. Text: after the aerobic week "there was a significant depression of aerobic potential (VO2 max), the restoration of which was observed over a 72 hour period. At the same time, anaerobic potential, assessed by a swimming test of 4 x 50m, restored quickly and exceeded its initial level. In the second case, restoration of anaerobic productivity took longer and exceeded its initial level after 72 hours. It is interesting that, during this time, aerobic potential rose over a 12 hour span and then diminished."
    20	   Figure values (read by eye, "about"): aerobic week, VO2 max starts about 87% of initial, crosses 100% at about 36 h and reaches about 106-107% by 72 h; the curve labelled "Training effect" starts about 93%, reaches 100% by about 12-24 h and sits about 101-102% at 72 h. Anaerobic week, VO2 max jumps to about 112-113% by about 12 h and falls to about 106% by 72 h; "Training effect" starts about 96% and crosses 100% at about 30-36 h, reaching about 102-103% at 72 h.
    21	3. **A speed-strength week (Fig 6.37, PDF p. 389, Mironenko 1979).** Bars: day 1 technique (medium), day 2 speed-strength (medium), day 3 speed-strength (high), day 4 complex (low), day 5 speed-strength (medium), day 6 speed-strength (high), day 7 empty. The text says these microcycles combine "workouts with large and moderate volumes of strength loading" with "workouts with an emphasis on technical and complex training" (PDF pp. 388-389).
    22	
    23	The authors close: "the microcycles used years ago have become the weakest link in the programming of training. Naturally, the preceding examples still do not eliminate those insufficiencies, although they point the way in which scientific research should be directed" (PDF p. 389).
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for the mixed week's failure is that the body "cannot simultaneously differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading" (PDF p. 387). For the single-emphasis weeks they report the restoration curves without explaining them.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Designing a loading week where one quality should be pushed: concentrate workouts of one emphasis in the week and expect roughly three days for the stressed quality to come back above baseline in the swimmers' data. Eric's baseline: "The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: the swimmers' VO2 max took about 72 h to recover after an aerobic-emphasis week, the same window Eric leaves before kickoff; this is a coincidence of numbers from a different sport and quality, not support for the football rule.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Unclear spots.** The text says anaerobic productivity "exceeded its initial level after 72 hours" in the anaerobic week, but the figure's "Training effect" curve crosses 100% at about 30-36 h; the figure also labels that curve "Training effect," not anaerobic potential, so which curve is the 4 x 50 m test is inferred from the text. The text says aerobic potential "rose over a 12 hour span and then diminished," but the figure shows it still about 6% above initial at 72 h. No sample sizes, athlete numbers or units for the "training load" bars are given. These are elite swimmers and a Soviet-era report; the speed-strength week has no outcome data at all.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors' own example is the Kudelin swimmer data above (PDF p. 388).
    32	
    33	**Related** — [[claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes]], [[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]], [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]], [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]]

    12	---
    13	
    14	# Speed Sports: No Speed Work During the Strength Block, Speed Starts as the Delayed Effect Rises, and Glycolytic Loading Has Two Peaks
    15	
    16	**What it is** — For "speed sports with a cyclical movement structure" (Fig 6.32b caption, PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372) the authors separate strength and speed more sharply than in speed-strength sports (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; both pages checked against the images):
    17	1. **Speed out of the block.** "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage. However, it is possible during this stage to perfect the athlete's motor skill, which directly determines high speed of movement." That skill is intermuscular coordination with "no tension in the muscle groups which do not directly take part in executing the motor tasks," and "This type of work is quite compatible with the athlete's decreased functional state, provided it is executed in the optimal range of intensity of effort and frequency of movement."
    18	2. **Speed starts with the LDTE.** "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE of strength loading (when the 'State' curve rises above the time axis), together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity."
    19	3. **Two anaerobic-glycolytic peaks.** High competition speed "is determined largely by specific speed-endurance." The glycolytic loading "exhibits two peaks": the first "is timed to end near the conclusion of the stage of concentrated strength loading. Specialised strength means are employed and the objective is to develop special strength-endurance which is primarily of a local nature"; the second "follows the period during which volume of speed work reaches a peak. Distance methods (in cyclic sports) or specialised means and methods (in one-on-one events and team sports) are employed... this type of work should be done in segments of small volume and combined with speed work."
    20	4. **Protect explosive strength.** "Along with the rise in strength-endurance, explosive strength tends to decrease when the second peak of the anaerobic-glycolytic loading occurs. Therefore, in those sports where explosive strength is of great importance, it is necessary to include a sufficiently intensive, small volume of maintenance loading."
    21	
    22	Fig 6.32(b), read from the image (PDF p. 383, no numeric scale): a shaded concentrated strength wave on the left; most curves (Vmax, S-E, Speed, STATE, An-Gly) dip or stay low during it and rise after it ends, with Vmax ending highest at the right. Individual curves are hard to follow where they cross.
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors give the reason for allowing coordination work during the block (it is compatible with a lowered functional state) and for the maintenance dose (explosive strength falls during the second glycolytic peak). They do not explain why speed must be excluded entirely rather than reduced. Inference: it follows from their rule that high-intensity work needs a fresh, not a depressed, functional state ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Cyclic speed sports such as sprinting, and by the authors' mention of "team sports" for the second glycolytic peak, sports where repeated speed matters. Eric's baseline: "For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 116, Explicit, claimed again as Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors program two deliberate glycolytic peaks, which goes further than the baseline; their own caution (small segments combined with speed work, a maintenance dose for explosive strength) is the part that fits the baseline best.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — Speed-strength and complex-technical sports keep some technique and do not separate speed so sharply ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Eric's baseline also says "staff do program it in the off-season" for glycolytic work (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)), so the conflict with line 116 is about in-season emphasis. No volumes, durations or intensities are given for either glycolytic peak.
    29	
    30	**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a 200 m sprinter spends a concentrated strength block doing strength-endurance circuits and relaxed technical drills with no sprinting, starts sprint work as the block ends, and adds short speed-endurance runs only after sprint volume has peaked, with a few explosive lifts kept in each week.
    31	
    32	**Related** — [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[principle--speed-strength-strength-endurance-and-speed-endurance-are-independent-qualities]], [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]

    13	
    14	# Tabachnik's Model Characteristics for 10.0 s Men and 11.0 s Women 100 m Sprinters: Speed, Relative Strength and Jump Targets
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two tables from Tabachnik (1979) give the profile a sprinter should reach to run 10.0 s (men) or 11.0 s (women) (PDF p. 392 / printed p. 381; every value below checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Table 6.8** (men 10.0 s / women 11.0 s):
    19	- General data: initial 100 m time 11.62 / 13.0 s; age of beginning sprinting 14.6 / 14.1 years; years of sprinting 8.4 / 8.3.
    20	- Speed indicators: simple motor reaction time 0.110 / 0.121; starting reaction time 0.136 / 0.149; total starting time 0.37 / 0.40 s; 5 m from low start 1.18 / 1.32; 30 m from low start 3.80 / 4.25; 50 m from low start 5.70 / 6.15; last 50 m of 100 m 4.45 / 5.00 s.
    21	- Relative muscular strength (relative to bodymass): trunk extension 2.80 / 2.60; trunk flexion 1.20 / 1.15; knee extension 2.20 / 2.00; knee flexion 1.10 / 1.05; hip extension 3.10 / 2.80; hip flexion 1.20 / 1.05; ankle plantarflexion 3.00 / 2.80.
    22	- Speed-strength: standing long jump 3.20 / 2.80 m; standing triple jump 10.0 / 8.40 m; ten-step jump from standing start 36.0 / 32.0 m.
    23	
    24	**Table 6.9** (section times by goal, seconds): for a 10.0 s goal, 15 m 1.16-1.18, 30 m 3.70-3.80, first 50 m 5.60-5.70, second 50 m 4.30-4.40, last 10 m 0.900; for 10.9 s, 15 m 1.30-1.32, 30 m 4.20-4.30, first 50 m 6.00-6.10, second 50 m 4.80-4.90, last 10 m 0.990 (goals 10.2, 10.5 and 10.7 s lie between).
    25	
    26	The tables sit among the authors' examples of descriptive modelling, alongside middle-distance (Tables 6.7, 6.10, Maximenko 1979), javelin (Table 6.11, Konstantinov 1978) and juvenile sprinter norms (Table 6.12, Alabin & Yushkevitch 1978) (PDF pp. 392-393).
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation, sample or method for the norms, and does not say how the relative-strength values were measured (the units are "relative to bodymass" only). The authors' general claim is that such norms "enable the coach to identify any weaknesses in the state of the athlete" (PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380).
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — As a reference for what a world-class sprint profile looked like in this Soviet model, and as a template for building one's own position-specific norm table. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: a table like this only earns a place if each row answers a programming question for the roster.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — **Internal inconsistencies, recorded as printed.** In Table 6.8 the men's 50 m from a low start (5.70 s) plus the last 50 m (4.45 s) sum to 10.15 s, not 10.0 s; Table 6.9 gives 4.30-4.40 s for the second 50 m at a 10.0 s goal, faster than Table 6.8's 4.45 s. Women's 6.15 + 5.00 = 11.15 s against an 11.0 s goal. The sources may define the splits differently, but the book does not say. Hand timing and 1970s testing methods are not described, so the values do not convert directly to modern electronic timing. These are elite sprinters, not football players; the relative-strength values come from an unspecified test and cannot be compared with force-plate or 1RM data.
    33	
    34	**Example** — The authors' own example is the table itself. Inference: a coach reading the standing triple jump target (10.0 m for 10.0 s men) would check whether a sprinter with fast 30 m times but a short triple jump lacks the speed-strength the model expects.
    35	
    36	**Related** — [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]], [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]

The body cannot simultaneously differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading... this form of microcycle construction enables one to achieve a large volume of loading, but the absence of any marked supercompensation (as revealed by the trend of restoration curve) shows that it fails to produce a definite increase in speed, aerobic or anaerobic productivity" (PDF pp. 387-388).
    19	2. **Single-emphasis swimming weeks (Fig 6.36, PDF p. 388; caption credits "Kubelin, 1980," the text and PDF p. 381 spell it "Kudelin").** Each week has three aerobic (or three anaerobic) workouts on days 1, 3 and 6, with speed-strength, complex and speed-endurance workouts on days 2, 4 and 5, and day 7 empty. Text: after the aerobic week "there was a significant depression of aerobic potential (VO2 max), the restoration of which was observed over a 72 hour period. At the same time, anaerobic potential, assessed by a swimming test of 4 x 50m, restored quickly and exceeded its initial level. In the second case, restoration of anaerobic productivity took longer and exceeded its initial level after 72 hours. It is interesting that, during this time, aerobic potential rose over a 12 hour span and then diminished."
    20	   Figure values (read by eye, "about"): aerobic week, VO2 max starts about 87% of initial, crosses 100% at about 36 h and reaches about 106-107% by 72 h; the curve labelled "Training effect" starts about 93%, reaches 100% by about 12-24 h and sits about 101-102% at 72 h. Anaerobic week, VO2 max jumps to about 112-113% by about 12 h and falls to about 106% by 72 h; "Training effect" starts about 96% and crosses 100% at about 30-36 h, reaching about 102-103% at 72 h.
    21	3. **A speed-strength week (Fig 6.37, PDF p. 389, Mironenko 1979).** Bars: day 1 technique (medium), day 2 speed-strength (medium), day 3 speed-strength (high), day 4 complex (low), day 5 speed-strength (medium), day 6 speed-strength (high), day 7 empty. The text says these microcycles combine "workouts with large and moderate volumes of strength loading" with "workouts with an emphasis on technical and complex training" (PDF pp. 388-389).
    22	
    23	The authors close: "the microcycles used years ago have become the weakest link in the programming of training. Naturally, the preceding examples still do not eliminate those insufficiencies, although they point the way in which scientific research should be directed" (PDF p. 389).
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reason for the mixed week's failure is that the body "cannot simultaneously differentiate between and accumulate specific reactions to every type of daily loading" (PDF p. 387). For the single-emphasis weeks they report the restoration curves without explaining them.
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Designing a loading week where one quality should be pushed: concentrate workouts of one emphasis in the week and expect roughly three days for the stressed quality to come back above baseline in the swimmers' data. Eric's baseline: "The in-season game week: Sunday off; Monday heavy lift; Tuesday and Wednesday heavy practice, with a lighter lift Wednesday; lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)). Inference: the swimmers' VO2 max took about 72 h to recover after an aerobic-emphasis week, the same window Eric leaves before kickoff; this is a coincidence of numbers from a different sport and quality, not support for the football rule.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — **Unclear spots.** The text says anaerobic productivity "exceeded its initial level after 72 hours" in the anaerobic week, but the figure's "Training effect" curve crosses 100% at about 30-36 h; the figure also labels that curve "Training effect," not anaerobic potential, so which curve is the 4 x 50 m test is inferred from the text. The text says aerobic potential "rose over a 12 hour span and then diminished," but the figure shows it still about 6% above initial at 72 h. No sample sizes, athlete numbers or units for the "training load" bars are given. These are elite swimmers and a Soviet-era report; the speed-strength week has no outcome data at all.
    30	
    31	**Example** — The authors' own example is the Kudelin swimmer data above (PDF p. 388).
    32	
    33	**Related** — [[claim--complex-training-falls-short-for-highly-qualified-athletes]], [[framework--mesocycle-variants-smooth-rise-versus-concentrated-dip-and-rebound]], [[periodization--bompa/heuristic--fatigue-fitness-3to1-ratio]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--microcycle-types-and-load-wave-design]], [[block-periodization--issurin/case-study--popov-aerobic-strength-microcycle]]
#### framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.12.2"
     7	topic: speed sport block organisation
     8	category: [speed, concentrated-loading, speed-endurance, anaerobic-glycolytic, periodization, cyclic-sports]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Speed Sports: No Speed Work During the Strength Block, Speed Starts as the Delayed Effect Rises, and Glycolytic Loading Has Two Peaks
    15	
    16	**What it is** — For "speed sports with a cyclical movement structure" (Fig 6.32b caption, PDF p. 383 / printed p. 372) the authors separate strength and speed more sharply than in speed-strength sports (PDF p. 384 / printed p. 373; both pages checked against the images):
    17	1. **Speed out of the block.** "Speed work is excluded totally from the concentrated strength loading stage. However, it is possible during this stage to perfect the athlete's motor skill, which directly determines high speed of movement." That skill is intermuscular coordination with "no tension in the muscle groups which do not directly take part in executing the motor tasks," and "This type of work is quite compatible with the athlete's decreased functional state, provided it is executed in the optimal range of intensity of effort and frequency of movement."
    18	2. **Speed starts with the LDTE.** "Speed work begins only at the beginning of the LDTE of strength loading (when the 'State' curve rises above the time axis), together with the necessary gradual rise in the training intensity."
    19	3. **Two anaerobic-glycolytic peaks.** High competition speed "is determined largely by specific speed-endurance." The glycolytic loading "exhibits two peaks": the first "is timed to end near the conclusion of the stage of concentrated strength loading. Specialised strength means are employed and the objective is to develop special strength-endurance which is primarily of a local nature"; the second "follows the period during which volume of speed work reaches a peak. Distance methods (in cyclic sports) or specialised means and methods (in one-on-one events and team sports) are employed... this type of work should be done in segments of small volume and combined with speed work."
    20	4. **Protect explosive strength.** "Along with the rise in strength-endurance, explosive strength tends to decrease when the second peak of the anaerobic-glycolytic loading occurs. Therefore, in those sports where explosive strength is of great importance, it is necessary to include a sufficiently intensive, small volume of maintenance loading."
    21	
    22	Fig 6.32(b), read from the image (PDF p. 383, no numeric scale): a shaded concentrated strength wave on the left; most curves (Vmax, S-E, Speed, STATE, An-Gly) dip or stay low during it and rise after it ends, with Vmax ending highest at the right. Individual curves are hard to follow where they cross.
    23	
    24	**Why it works** — The authors give the reason for allowing coordination work during the block (it is compatible with a lowered functional state) and for the maintenance dose (explosive strength falls during the second glycolytic peak). They do not explain why speed must be excluded entirely rather than reduced. Inference: it follows from their rule that high-intensity work needs a fresh, not a depressed, functional state ([[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]]).
    25	
    26	**When to apply** — Cyclic speed sports such as sprinting, and by the authors' mention of "team sports" for the second glycolytic peak, sports where repeated speed matters. Eric's baseline: "For football specifically, the stated priority stack is: Goal 1, alactic and aerobic capacity/power for fall-camp demands; Goal 2, the same two systems for game demands; glycolytic conditioning is treated as a "worst case scenario" to be absorbed incidentally through camp and practice rather than programmed as a primary target" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 116, Explicit, claimed again as Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q1)). Inference: the authors program two deliberate glycolytic peaks, which goes further than the baseline; their own caution (small segments combined with speed work, a maintenance dose for explosive strength) is the part that fits the baseline best.
    27	
    28	**When NOT to apply** — Speed-strength and complex-technical sports keep some technique and do not separate speed so sharply ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Eric's baseline also says "staff do program it in the off-season" for glycolytic work (line 117, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q19)), so the conflict with line 116 is about in-season emphasis. No volumes, durations or intensities are given for either glycolytic peak.
    29	
    30	**Example** — The authors give the schematic only. Inference: a 200 m sprinter spends a concentrated strength block doing strength-endurance circuits and relaxed technical drills with no sprinting, starts sprint work as the block ends, and adds short speed-endurance runs only after sprint volume has peaked, with a few explosive lifts kept in each week.
    31	
    32	**Related** — [[heuristic--technique-work-during-and-after-a-concentrated-strength-block]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[principle--speed-strength-strength-endurance-and-speed-endurance-are-independent-qualities]], [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[framework--conjugate-sequence-system-of-training-means]]
#### case-study--tabachnik-100m-sprinter-model-characteristics
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: case-study
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.14"
     7	topic: sprinter model characteristics
     8	category: [sprinting, sports-modelling, testing-norms, relative-strength, speed-strength]
     9	confidence: untested
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Tabachnik's Model Characteristics for 10.0 s Men and 11.0 s Women 100 m Sprinters: Speed, Relative Strength and Jump Targets
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two tables from Tabachnik (1979) give the profile a sprinter should reach to run 10.0 s (men) or 11.0 s (women) (PDF p. 392 / printed p. 381; every value below checked against the page image).
    17	
    18	**Table 6.8** (men 10.0 s / women 11.0 s):
    19	- General data: initial 100 m time 11.62 / 13.0 s; age of beginning sprinting 14.6 / 14.1 years; years of sprinting 8.4 / 8.3.
    20	- Speed indicators: simple motor reaction time 0.110 / 0.121; starting reaction time 0.136 / 0.149; total starting time 0.37 / 0.40 s; 5 m from low start 1.18 / 1.32; 30 m from low start 3.80 / 4.25; 50 m from low start 5.70 / 6.15; last 50 m of 100 m 4.45 / 5.00 s.
    21	- Relative muscular strength (relative to bodymass): trunk extension 2.80 / 2.60; trunk flexion 1.20 / 1.15; knee extension 2.20 / 2.00; knee flexion 1.10 / 1.05; hip extension 3.10 / 2.80; hip flexion 1.20 / 1.05; ankle plantarflexion 3.00 / 2.80.
    22	- Speed-strength: standing long jump 3.20 / 2.80 m; standing triple jump 10.0 / 8.40 m; ten-step jump from standing start 36.0 / 32.0 m.
    23	
    24	**Table 6.9** (section times by goal, seconds): for a 10.0 s goal, 15 m 1.16-1.18, 30 m 3.70-3.80, first 50 m 5.60-5.70, second 50 m 4.30-4.40, last 10 m 0.900; for 10.9 s, 15 m 1.30-1.32, 30 m 4.20-4.30, first 50 m 6.00-6.10, second 50 m 4.80-4.90, last 10 m 0.990 (goals 10.2, 10.5 and 10.7 s lie between).
    25	
    26	The tables sit among the authors' examples of descriptive modelling, alongside middle-distance (Tables 6.7, 6.10, Maximenko 1979), javelin (Table 6.11, Konstantinov 1978) and juvenile sprinter norms (Table 6.12, Alabin & Yushkevitch 1978) (PDF pp. 392-393).
    27	
    28	**Why it works** — The book gives no derivation, sample or method for the norms, and does not say how the relative-strength values were measured (the units are "relative to bodymass" only). The authors' general claim is that such norms "enable the coach to identify any weaknesses in the state of the athlete" (PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380).
    29	
    30	**When to apply** — As a reference for what a world-class sprint profile looked like in this Soviet model, and as a template for building one's own position-specific norm table. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: a table like this only earns a place if each row answers a programming question for the roster.
    31	
    32	**When NOT to apply** — **Internal inconsistencies, recorded as printed.** In Table 6.8 the men's 50 m from a low start (5.70 s) plus the last 50 m (4.45 s) sum to 10.15 s, not 10.0 s; Table 6.9 gives 4.30-4.40 s for the second 50 m at a 10.0 s goal, faster than Table 6.8's 4.45 s. Women's 6.15 + 5.00 = 11.15 s against an 11.0 s goal. The sources may define the splits differently, but the book does not say. Hand timing and 1970s testing methods are not described, so the values do not convert directly to modern electronic timing. These are elite sprinters, not football players; the relative-strength values come from an unspecified test and cannot be compared with force-plate or 1RM data.
    33	
    34	**Example** — The authors' own example is the table itself. Inference: a coach reading the standing triple jump target (10.0 m for 10.0 s men) would check whether a sprinter with fast 30 m times but a short triple jump lacks the speed-strength the model expects.
    35	
    36	**Related** — [[framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models]], [[transfer-of-training-in-sports--bondarchuk/claim--model-characteristic-tables-exist-by-qualification]], [[claim--absolute-leg-strength-connects-to-sprint-speed-only-indirectly-via-jump]]

#### framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models
     1	---
     2	type: library-entry
     3	kind: framework
     4	domain: strength-and-conditioning
     5	book: supertraining--verkhoshansky
     6	chapter: "6.14"
     7	topic: sports modelling
     8	category: [sports-modelling, needs-analysis, annual-plan, testing, programming]
     9	confidence: supported
    10	ingest-tier: full-text
    11	created: 2026-10-03
    12	---
    13	
    14	# Sports Modelling: a Descriptive Model of the Sport Feeds a Prescriptive Model of the Athlete's State and the Loading Programme
    15	
    16	**What it is** — The authors split the models needed to design programmes into two classes (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image):
    17	- **The descriptive model** "furnishes qualitative details of the motor qualities and fitness factors needed for proficiency in a given sport, as well as desirable quantitative kinanthropometric, kinesiological, physiological and biomechanical details which characterise movement at all stages of that sport." Examples of its contents: "movement patterns, velocities and accelerations at different joint angles or stages of an event, reaction time, 'lactate threshold' (OBLA), relative muscle strength, body proportions, agonist/antagonist muscle strength ratios and timing of segments of important movements."
    18	- **The prescriptive model** "represents a simplified analogue of the actual training process, omitting some details, but preserving the essential information concerning its composition and structure. It describes the dynamics of the athlete's fitness state and the systems of organising annual training." Its core is a model of the athlete's state that "diagramatically expresses the optimal changes in the most important indicators of special work capacity over time" and "determines the specific periods when one should plan to achieve peak levels." It "draws strongly on the data furnished by the descriptive model."
    19	- Each can be **qualitative** (the dynamics of the functional indicators, the main training contents and how components connect) or **quantitative** ("all numerical aspects of the training... such as calculation of volume, intensity, duration of stages and loading distribution in different intensity zones").
    20	
    21	Conventions for the 6.14 annual models (PDF pp. 390-391 / printed pp. 379-380, checked against the page images): months are not named because summer and winter sports are covered; "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period"; each model pairs a fitness-state diagram with a loading diagram; "One can use any method that enables one to measure the values of these indicators"; "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE"; the rectangular blocks are schematic, since "the actual loading follows a concentrated wave pattern which gradually reaches a peak, then subsides in volume"; and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar.
    22	
    23	On measurement: "It is of little value to identify which energy systems, types of fitness or movement patterns are involved in a sport unless accurate numerical determinations are regularly made of each of these factors. Even then, we have to remember that the body is not simply a machine in which input and output are deterministically related, but an organism whose behaviour displays non-linearity and fairly random deviations... Nevertheless, without this information, long-term programming becomes imprecise" (PDF p. 391, checked against the page image). The descriptive-modelling passage names the "Multifactorial Fitness Profile (MFP) discussed later... (Ch 7)" and says "Many years of Russian research have produced models for every type of sport" (PDF pp. 390-391). Inference: the passage reads as Siff's framing of the Russian material.
    24	
    25	**Why it works** — The authors' reason is control: modelling "makes it possible to manage the organisational complexity of sports activities and devise a practical scheme for describing and controlling the training process" (PDF p. 390), and norms "enable the coach to identify any weaknesses in the state of the athlete and thereby modify the training programme" (PDF p. 391).
    26	
    27	**When to apply** — Before writing an annual plan: build or borrow a descriptive model of what the sport demands, with numbers, then draw the planned course of the key indicators across the year and the loading that should produce it. Eric's baseline: "If it doesn't answer a question anyone has, or a direct need, then it doesn't have a place" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 32, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q3)). Inference: the descriptive model is one way to state those questions in advance, so each test in the battery is tied to a factor the model says matters.
    28	
    29	**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves warn that the body is non-linear and deviates "fairly random[ly]" from quantitative prediction, so a model is a guide, not a forecast.     12	---
    13	
    14	# In a Long Monocyclic Competition Period, a Prolonged Cut in Loading Volume Lowers Fitness; Competition Plus Small Special Loads Cannot Maintain It
    15	
    16	**What it is** — In the long-duration endurance model (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385, checked against the page image): "It has been established that the prolonged reduction in the volume of loading during the competition period (with monocyclic periodisation) leads to re-adaptation at a lower level, which is reflected in the drop of non-specific trainability. Competition and special supplementary loading (with limited volumes) cannot stimulate further development or even maintain special work-capacity. Thus, it is appropriate to periodically increase the volume of competition and special assistance loading (Baranovsky, 1969; Kryazh, 1969; Muzis, 1970; Zhikharevich, 1976)." The paired condition from Gilyazova (1978) is that stable results need "not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period" and a gradual preparatory increase ("a mean monthly increase of 7-14%") (PDF p. 396).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is "re-adaptation at a lower level": the body adapts down to the reduced load. They give no physiological detail and no data beyond the four citations.
    19	
    20	**When to apply** — Long competition periods (the model's is "some 4-5 months," PDF p. 396) in which the athlete would otherwise only compete and do light maintenance: build in periodic increases in special and assistance volume. Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Also: "In-season programming deliberately waves volume and intensity even when the practice schedule looks repetitive week to week, specifically to avoid training monotony for the athlete" (line 181, Inferred (transcript)). Inference: the authors' warning is against a *prolonged* volume cut in a long season; the baseline's in-season waving, and the bye-week "speed and strength top-up" (line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)), are the kind of periodic volume increase the authors call for. A football season of games is shorter than the model's 4-5 month competition period, and the sport is not an endurance sport.
    21	
    22	**When NOT to apply** — The statement is made for long-duration endurance sports under monocyclic periodisation; the authors do not extend it to strength or team sports. It does not mean intensity can be dropped. In the explosive-strength model the second strength block deliberately carries less volume than the first ("It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383), so the rule applies to special and competition loading in endurance sport, not to every quality in every sport.
    23	
    24	**Example** — The authors give no worked case. Inference: a marathoner in a five-month racing season returns every few weeks to a higher-volume week of race-pace and assistance work instead of only racing and easy running between races.
    25	
    26	**Related** — [[framework--annual-models-for-medium-and-long-duration-endurance-sports]], [[block-periodization--issurin/claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]], [[block-periodization--issurin/framework--in-season-team-sport-mini-block-microcycle]]

    13	
    14	# Follow a High-Volume, Low-Intensity Concentrated Block With Moderate-Volume Explosive Work to Enlarge the Delayed Training Effect
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under the heading "More Advanced Use of Concentrated Loading" (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image) the authors modify the separated-block models of 6.14: "in speed-strength sports, the magnitude of the delayed training effect (LDTE) may be enhanced further if the concentrated loading is followed by specialised work of moderate volume, which includes higher power or more explosive muscle contraction regimes, such as jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts." The loads overlap: "There is an overlapping of the different training volumes, which peak smoothly in each case to ensure optimal increase in the LDTE" (PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387). In the bi-cyclic version, "stages A and C refer to concentrated periods of high volume, low intensity work and stages B and D to moderate volumes of specialised, higher intensity speed-strength work. This scheme has been recommended to ensure continuous increase in special strength over a long period (Verkhoshansky, 1978)" (PDF p. 398).
    17	
    18	The figures, read from the page images (no numeric axes):
    19	- **Fig 6.43** (PDF p. 398, monocyclic large mesocycle): a tall wave A in the preparatory phase, a smaller wave B starting as A falls and peaking at about the start of the competition phase. The speed-strength curve sags while A is high, then rises through B and keeps rising into the competition phase.
    20	- **Fig 6.44** (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, bi-cyclic): tall A, small B, tall C, small D in sequence. Speed-strength dips during A, rises during B, flattens or dips slightly during C, and rises again after it to its highest level at the right.
    21	- **Fig 6.45** (PDF p. 399, a large mesocycle for speed-strength sports): the text says "the concentrated strength loading block occupies the first half of the large mesocycle, following the groundwork laid by general physical preparation (GPP) and the peak amount of aerobic work... Technique and speed training occupies the second half." The figure shows an aerobic-work curve peaking early, a large shaded wave over the first half, a second shaded wave over the second half labelled "Technique and Speed," and a fitness-state curve that dips then rises to its highest point at the right.
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — The authors give a principle rather than a measured mechanism: overlapping loads that "peak smoothly" serve the LDTE, and "the inclusion of regular passive and active restoration periods between stages of greater loading is important to facilitate development of the LDTE" (PDF p. 398). They also argue for putting the bulk of strength work early: "Since large volumes of strength and technique training generally are incompatible, the greatest quantity of strength work should be done during the preparatory period, with more emphasis being placed on technique work during the competitive phase when the LDTE rises markedly" (PDF p. 399). No data are shown; the figures are schematics credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — Speed-strength athletes coming out of a high-volume strength block: bring in moderate volumes of jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts as the block tapers, rather than dropping straight to technique and speed alone. The authors say the boundaries are loose: "stage B does not necessarily begin where shown, but may commence far earlier, while stage A may tail off right near the end of phase B" (PDF p. 398; "phase B" is printed as such). The authors tie this to Matveyev's "non-discreteness of the preparatory and competitive phases": "it is sometimes perfectly appropriate to have elements of each intermingled in various 'doses'" (PDF p. 398). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the A-then-B wave is one way to stage that shift within one off-season.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is stated for speed-strength sports. It assumes the A stage is "high volume, low intensity," consistent with the low-intensity condition for concentrated loading ([[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]); an A stage built from heavy, intense lifting is a different situation the authors do not cover. **Unclear figure labels:** the caption of Fig 6.45 says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading, while B and C refer to the types of training identified in the diagram," but in the figure the label "GPP" sits under wave A and "Strength Load" sits under wave B (PDF p. 399). Fig 6.46 has the same mismatch (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389). Which wave is the strength block cannot be settled from the page. No dose for the B stage is given beyond "moderate volume."
    28	
    29	**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: after a four-week block of high-volume, moderate-load squats, pulls and loaded jumps, a jumper adds two short weekly sessions of bounding, a few depth jumps and one or two near-maximal lifts, with that work peaking about when the first competitions begin.

    13	
    14	# Annual Models for Endurance Sports: Bi-Cyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Medium Duration, Monocyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Long Duration
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two prescriptive models from 6.14.2 and 6.14.3 (PDF pp. 395-397 / printed pp. 384-386; text and Figs 6.40 and 6.41 checked against the page images; Fig 6.46 on PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).
    17	
    18	**Medium-duration endurance (bi-cyclic, Fig 6.40).**
    19	- Two mesocycles and two competition stages; in the first "one need not compete at the fundamental distance," but can compete "at other distances," which "simultaneously serve as control estimates of the athlete's level of aerobic and anaerobic capacity" (PDF p. 395).
    20	- "Explosive strength peaks at the beginning of the second competition stage, after which it decreases, together with the rise in the volume of intense (anaerobic-glycolytic) cyclic work." Anaerobic capacity and strength-endurance "reach their highest levels during the most important competitive stage (10th - 11th months)" (PDF p. 395).
    21	- Aerobic loading predominates in the first preparatory stage; "during the second stage the work is chiefly at the OBLA (onset of blood lactate accumulation) level"; aerobic volume rises again in the second competition stage "to promote restoration." Speed work (ATP-CP) and speed-endurance (glycolytic) are timed for the LDTE stage, "i.e. the development of speed precedes that of speed-endurance." Overall sequence: "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" (PDF p. 395).
    22	- Strength block contents: "The first block emphasizes the development of explosive strength and local muscular endurance, while the second emphasizes mainly local muscular endurance" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385).
    23	- Fig 6.40, read by eye: block 1 over about months 2-4 (taller), block 2 over about months 6-7 (shorter); phases I about months 1-4, II about month 5, III about months 6-8, IV about months 9-11. For a large mesocycle (Fig 6.46, PDF pp. 399-400), aerobic training "covers the first half of the large mesocycle during which the GPP and concentrated strength loading take place," then speed, then specialised endurance, with competitions as a main way to develop it.
    24	
    25	**Long-duration endurance (monocyclic, Fig 6.41).**
    26	- "Competition in long duration events requires a long preparatory period (up to 6 months) for creating stable adaptation to preserve the special work-capacity for some 4-5 months during the competitive period" (PDF p. 396).
    27	- Stable results come "if the increase in loading during the preparatory period occurs gradually (a mean monthly increase of 7-14%), if there is not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period, and if the portion of loading in the zone of anaerobic energy production is not increased (Gilyazova, 1978)" (PDF p. 396). See [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]].
    28	- "Within a monocycle of periodisation, it provides a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training": "The first block contains general conditioning strength work, while the second block emphasizes the development of local muscular endurance," carrying work capacity "right up to the important competitions in the 10th and 11th months" (PDF p. 396).
    29	- Fig 6.41, read by eye: phase I about months 1-6, phase II about months 6-11; block 1 over about months 2-3, block 2 over about months 6-7. Aerobic capacity peaks around the start of the competition period and then eases, as the text says ("maximum aerobic productivity at the beginning of the competition period, and some decrease," PDF p. 397).
    30	
    31	**Why it works** — Both models rest on the LDTE of concentrated strength blocks and on timing speed and speed-endurance after them. The only cited data are Gilyazova (1978) for the monocyclic loading conditions; the figures are schematics (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
    32	
    33	**When to apply** — Annual planning for middle-distance (medium) or long-distance (long) endurance athletes who use strength blocks. Not a football model; the medium-duration sequence "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" is the transferable idea. Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once" and "priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 115, Explicit; the two phrases are joined by a dash in the baseline). Inference: both models pick one energy-system emphasis per stage in that spirit.
    34	
    35	**When NOT to apply** — Long-duration sports are given a monocycle, while the 6.13 aims call for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]] for this internal conflict. The models are for qualified athletes and carry the same Issurin 2016 challenge to concentrated loading as the other 6.14 models ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Fig 6.46's caption says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading," but the figure prints "GPP" under A and "Strength Load" under B; which wave is the strength block is unclear.
    36	
    37	**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: an 800 m runner competes at 400 m and 1500 m in the first competition stage as control tests, then runs the main 800 m season in months 10-11 after a smaller second block focused on local muscular endurance.
    38	
    39	**Related** — [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]], [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]], [[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]], [[framework--speed-sport-block-organisation-and-two-glycolytic-peaks]], [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]], [[principle--local-muscular-endurance-adaptation-is-specific-to-the-trained-muscles]]

28:**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin** for team sports. The book says concentrated strength loading was confirmed in "team sports" (PDF p. 382); the library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6). The paired condition from Gilyazova (1978) is that stable results need "not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period" and a gradual preparatory increase ("a mean monthly increase of 7-14%") (PDF p. 396).
    17	
    18	**Why it works** — The authors' explanation is "re-adaptation at a lower level": the body adapts down to the reduced load. They give no physiological detail and no data beyond the four citations.
    19

Inference: the authors' warning is against a *prolonged* volume cut in a long season; the baseline's in-season waving, and the bye-week "speed and strength top-up" (line 187, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q17)), are the kind of periodic volume increase the authors call for. A football season of games is shorter than the model's 4-5 month competition period, and the sport is not an endurance sport.

    22	**When NOT to apply** — The statement is made for long-duration endurance sports under monocyclic periodisation; the authors do not extend it to strength or team sports. It does not mean intensity can be dropped. In the explosive-strength model the second strength block deliberately carries less volume than the first ("It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work," PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383), so the rule applies to special and competition loading in endurance sport, not to every quality in every sport.

    14	# Follow a High-Volume, Low-Intensity Concentrated Block With Moderate-Volume Explosive Work to Enlarge the Delayed Training Effect
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Under the heading "More Advanced Use of Concentrated Loading" (PDF p. 397 / printed p. 386, checked against the page image) the authors modify the separated-block models of 6.14: "in speed-strength sports, the magnitude of the delayed training effect (LDTE) may be enhanced further if the concentrated loading is followed by specialised work of moderate volume, which includes higher power or more explosive muscle contraction regimes, such as jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts." The loads overlap: "There is an overlapping of the different training volumes, which peak smoothly in each case to ensure optimal increase in the LDTE" (PDF p. 398 / printed p. 387). In the bi-cyclic version, "stages A and C refer to concentrated periods of high volume, low intensity work and stages B and D to moderate volumes of specialised, higher intensity speed-strength work. This scheme has been recommended to ensure continuous increase in special strength over a long period (Verkhoshansky, 1978)" (PDF p. 398).
    17	
    18	The figures, read from the page images (no numeric axes):
    19	- **Fig 6.43** (PDF p. 398, monocyclic large mesocycle): a tall wave A in the preparatory phase, a smaller wave B starting as A falls and peaking at about the start of the competition phase. The speed-strength curve sags while A is high, then rises through B and keeps rising into the competition phase.
    20	- **Fig 6.44** (PDF p. 399 / printed p. 388, bi-cyclic): tall A, small B, tall C, small D in sequence. Speed-strength dips during A, rises during B, flattens or dips slightly during C, and rises again after it to its highest level at the right.
    21	- **Fig 6.45** (PDF p. 399, a large mesocycle for speed-strength sports): the text says "the concentrated strength loading block occupies the first half of the large mesocycle, following the groundwork laid by general physical preparation (GPP) and the peak amount of aerobic work... Technique and speed training occupies the second half." The figure shows an aerobic-work curve peaking early, a large shaded wave over the first half, a second shaded wave over the second half labelled "Technique and Speed," and a fitness-state curve that dips then rises to its highest point at the right.
    22	
    23	**Why it works** — The authors give a principle rather than a measured mechanism: overlapping loads that "peak smoothly" serve the LDTE, and "the inclusion of regular passive and active restoration periods between stages of greater loading is important to facilitate development of the LDTE" (PDF p. 398). They also argue for putting the bulk of strength work early: "Since large volumes of strength and technique training generally are incompatible, the greatest quantity of strength work should be done during the preparatory period, with more emphasis being placed on technique work during the competitive phase when the LDTE rises markedly" (PDF p. 399). No data are shown; the figures are schematics credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).
    24	
    25	**When to apply** — Speed-strength athletes coming out of a high-volume strength block: bring in moderate volumes of jumps, plyometrics and maximal attempts as the block tapers, rather than dropping straight to technique and speed alone. The authors say the boundaries are loose: "stage B does not necessarily begin where shown, but may commence far earlier, while stage A may tail off right near the end of phase B" (PDF p. 398; "phase B" is printed as such). The authors tie this to Matveyev's "non-discreteness of the preparatory and competitive phases": "it is sometimes perfectly appropriate to have elements of each intermingled in various 'doses'" (PDF p. 398). Eric's baseline: "Off-season strength work prioritizes relative strength and technique first; already-strong athletes shift more time toward strength-speed/speed-strength work" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: the A-then-B wave is one way to stage that shift within one off-season.
    26	
    27	**When NOT to apply** — The scheme is stated for speed-strength sports. It assumes the A stage is "high volume, low intensity," consistent with the low-intensity condition for concentrated loading ([[framework--conditions-for-concentrated-unidirectional-loading]]); an A stage built from heavy, intense lifting is a different situation the authors do not cover. **Unclear figure labels:** the caption of Fig 6.45 says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading, while B and C refer to the types of training identified in the diagram," but in the figure the label "GPP" sits under wave A and "Strength Load" sits under wave B (PDF p. 399). Fig 6.46 has the same mismatch (PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389). Which wave is the strength block cannot be settled from the page. No dose for the B stage is given beyond "moderate volume."
    28	
    29	**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: after a four-week block of high-volume, moderate-load squats, pulls and loaded jumps, a jumper adds two short weekly sessions of bounding, a few depth jumps and one or two near-maximal lifts, with that work peaking about when the first competitions begin.

    13	
    14	# Annual Models for Endurance Sports: Bi-Cyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Medium Duration, Monocyclic With Two Strength Blocks for Long Duration
    15	
    16	**What it is** — Two prescriptive models from 6.14.2 and 6.14.3 (PDF pp. 395-397 / printed pp. 384-386; text and Figs 6.40 and 6.41 checked against the page images; Fig 6.46 on PDF p. 400 / printed p. 389).
    17	
    18	**Medium-duration endurance (bi-cyclic, Fig 6.40).**
    19	- Two mesocycles and two competition stages; in the first "one need not compete at the fundamental distance," but can compete "at other distances," which "simultaneously serve as control estimates of the athlete's level of aerobic and anaerobic capacity" (PDF p. 395).
    20	- "Explosive strength peaks at the beginning of the second competition stage, after which it decreases, together with the rise in the volume of intense (anaerobic-glycolytic) cyclic work." Anaerobic capacity and strength-endurance "reach their highest levels during the most important competitive stage (10th - 11th months)" (PDF p. 395).
    21	- Aerobic loading predominates in the first preparatory stage; "during the second stage the work is chiefly at the OBLA (onset of blood lactate accumulation) level"; aerobic volume rises again in the second competition stage "to promote restoration." Speed work (ATP-CP) and speed-endurance (glycolytic) are timed for the LDTE stage, "i.e. the development of speed precedes that of speed-endurance." Overall sequence: "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" (PDF p. 395).
    22	- Strength block contents: "The first block emphasizes the development of explosive strength and local muscular endurance, while the second emphasizes mainly local muscular endurance" (PDF p. 396 / printed p. 385).
    23	- Fig 6.40, read by eye: block 1 over about months 2-4 (taller), block 2 over about months 6-7 (shorter); phases I about months 1-4, II about month 5, III about months 6-8, IV about months 9-11. For a large mesocycle (Fig 6.46, PDF pp. 399-400), aerobic training "covers the first half of the large mesocycle during which the GPP and concentrated strength loading take place," then speed, then specialised endurance, with competitions as a main way to develop it.
    24	
    25	**Long-duration endurance (monocyclic, Fig 6.41).**
    26	- "Competition in long duration events requires a long preparatory period (up to 6 months) for creating stable adaptation to preserve the special work-capacity for some 4-5 months during the competitive period" (PDF p. 396).
    27	- Stable results come "if the increase in loading during the preparatory period occurs gradually (a mean monthly increase of 7-14%), if there is not a sharp drop in the volume of loading during the competitive period, and if the portion of loading in the zone of anaerobic energy production is not increased (Gilyazova, 1978)" (PDF p. 396). See [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]].
    28	- "Within a monocycle of periodisation, it provides a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training": "The first block contains general conditioning strength work, while the second block emphasizes the development of local muscular endurance," carrying work capacity "right up to the important competitions in the 10th and 11th months" (PDF p. 396).
    29	- Fig 6.41, read by eye: phase I about months 1-6, phase II about months 6-11; block 1 over about months 2-3, block 2 over about months 6-7. Aerobic capacity peaks around the start of the competition period and then eases, as the text says ("maximum aerobic productivity at the beginning of the competition period, and some decrease," PDF p. 397).
    30	
    31	**Why it works** — Both models rest on the LDTE of concentrated strength blocks and on timing speed and speed-endurance after them. The only cited data are Gilyazova (1978) for the monocyclic loading conditions; the figures are schematics (Siff & Verkhoshansky, 1999).
    32	
    33	**When to apply** — Annual planning for middle-distance (medium) or long-distance (long) endurance athletes who use strength blocks. Not a football model; the medium-duration sequence "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" is the transferable idea. Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once" and "priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 115, Explicit; the two phrases are joined by a dash in the baseline). Inference: both models pick one energy-system emphasis per stage in that spirit.
    34	
    35	**When NOT to apply** — Long-duration sports are given a monocycle, while the 6.13 aims call for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]] for this internal conflict. The models are for qualified athletes and carry the same Issurin 2016 challenge to concentrated loading as the other 6.14 models ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Fig 6.46's caption says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading," but the figure prints "GPP" under A and "Strength Load" under B; which wave is the strength block is unclear.
    36	
    37	**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: an 800 m runner competes at 400 m and 1500 m in the first competition stage as control tests, then runs the main 800 m season in months 10-11 after a smaller second block focused on local muscular endurance.
    38

# The Training Stage (A-T-R + Competition) Is the Annual Plan's Building Block, Enabling Multiple Peaks

**What it is** — Issurin's annual cycle is built from a sequence of **training stages**,
each one containing all three mesocycle-blocks (accumulation, transmutation, realization) in
order, ending in a competition (PDF p. 38, printed p. 27). Each training stage "gives the
appearance of an annual cycle in miniature": a block resembling a preparatory period
(accumulation), one resembling a competition period (transmutation), and a tapering block
ending in competitive performance (realization) (PDF p. 39, printed p. 28). The duration of
a training stage is set by how long the constituent residual training effects can be
superimposed (Figure 1.8; see
[[claim--residual-training-effect-durations-by-motor-ability]]) and "should be about two
months," though Issurin notes stages can run shorter close to season peaking or longer
earlier in the season, in which case "special measures should be used to prolong residual
training effects" (developed in Chapter 3, now ingested; see
[[framework--prolonging-residual-effects-with-mini-blocks]] and `_book.md`).
The number of training stages in a season "usually varies from four to seven," depending on
the sport's competition calendar (PDF p. 40, printed p. 29, Figure 1.9). Issurin lists four

# World-Class Track and Field Athletes Compete and Peak Many Times Per Season, Not Once

**What it is** — Table 1.5 (PDF p. 24, printed p. 13, based on Suslov, 2001, with Issurin's
modifications) reports three world-class athletes' single-season competition patterns:
**Marion Jones** (100-200m, long jump; 1998 season) had **10 peaks** (8 in running, 2 in
long jump, all at personal-best level) across a **200-day** competitive span, with typical
19-22 day intervals between peaks. **Sergei Bubka** (pole vault; 1991 season) had **7
peaks** (all within 3% of his personal best, 595-612 cm) across a **265-day** span,
23-43 day intervals. **Stefka Kostadinova** (high jump; 1998 season) had **11 peaks** (all
within 3% of her personal best, 200-205 cm), 14-25 day intervals, across winter ~20 days and
spring/summer 135 days (**Inference:** 155 days combined; the table gives the two figures
separately, not a single summed span). Issurin's summary point, stated on the preceding page
(PDF p. 23, printed p. 12): these athletes' 5-8 month competitive spans "can not be
subdivided into traditional preparatory and competitive periods," yet their basic abilities
(max strength, aerobic regeneration capacity) still had to be maintained across that entire
span.
