lines: # Annual Model for Explosive-Strength Sports: Two Mesocycles, Two Concentrated Strength Blocks, the Second Smaller in Volume and Higher in Intensity

-**What it is** — The authors' prescriptive model for sports "requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383; Fig 6.39 on PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384; both pages checked against the page images, the figure also at 300 dpi). The text gives these rules:

+**What it is** — The authors' prescriptive model for sports "requiring explosive strength" (PDF p. 394 / printed p. 383; Fig 6.39 on PDF p. 395 / printed p. 384; both pages checked against the page images, the figure also at 400 dpi with crops of both panels). The text gives these rules:

1. **Bi-cyclic structure.** "This model involves bi-cyclic periodisation of training and includes two mesocycles aimed at optimally developing the body's current adaptation reserves and achieving the planned level of special-strength preparedness at the most important competitions." The fitness model tracks "absolute, explosive and starting strength indicators, the highest values of which are achieved at the end of each mesocycle" (PDF p. 394).

2. **Strength blocks against a background of speed and technique.** "The organisation of loading provides for exploiting the LDTE of the block of strength work in each mesocycle against a background of the fundamental speed and technical training. The basic principle is block loading with means of different primary emphasis." Technique is "not excluded during the strength loading block. However, such work is included at reduced intensity using the separate elements and their links (see 2.1.2), as well as the rhythmic patterns of individual phases" (PDF p. 394). LDTE is the book's long-term delayed training effect of concentrated strength loading.

3. **Second block: less volume, more intensity.** "The second strength block imposes a smaller volume, although the general loading intensity is higher than in the first block. Since the second block is executed against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle, the LDTE will be preserved during the second competitive stage. It is unnecessary at this time to further increase the volume of strength work, which can be used exclusively for preparing the neuromuscular system before the subsequent training that emphasizes technique or competitive readiness" (PDF p. 394).

4. **Block contents.** The blocks follow "the principle of preserving the training potential of the loading by means of the conjugate sequence system (5.3.3)" (PDF p. 394). The section just before 6.14.1 shows what a speed-strength block holds: "Jumping > Weights exercises > Plyometrics," "not sharply separated by time intervals, but substituted continuously for one another, ensuring that intensity and functional indicators are monitored carefully to avoid overtraining" (PDF p. 394; Fig 6.38, Verkhoshansky 1977). In Fig 6.38 the three overlapping volume waves are A jumps (early, small), B weights exercises (middle, the largest) and C plyometric depth jumps (late, small); read from the image, no numeric axis.

5. **GPP.** "Within each block, they offer variety and aid restoration after high volume strength loading, while at the LDTE stage, the GPP assists restoration after intense specialised loading... The largest relative volume of GPP means occurs during the competitive periods" (PDF p. 394). See [[heuristic--use-low-intensity-gpp-as-restoration-in-concentrated-loading-models]].

-**Fig 6.39, read from the image (all month values "about"; no vertical scale).** The time axis runs 11 months (the 6.14 conventions: "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period," PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379). Phases: I (1st preparation) about months 1-4, II (1st competition) about month 5, III (2nd preparation) about months 6-8, IV (2nd competition) about months 9-11. The phase boundaries and dashed lines do not fall exactly on the month ticks (phase I ends late in month 4; phase III ends during month 8). Block 1 is a tall shaded rectangle over about months 1-3; block 2 is a shorter rectangle over about months 6-7, roughly two thirds of block 1's height, matching the text's "smaller volume." Upper panel: all three strength curves (Starting, Explosive, Maximum) fall during block 1 after a small early bump in the two upper curves, rise to a first peak at about months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary), dip again during block 2 (about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross at about months 8-9, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, falls during block 2, then rises to its highest level at about months 9-10 and declines toward month 11. The GPP and Speed curves cross several times and cannot be told apart reliably in the image; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.

+**Fig 6.39, read from the image (all month values "about"; no vertical scale).** The time axis runs 11 months (the 6.14 conventions: "Each model consists of about 11 months, since, on average, one month is allotted for the final transition period," PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379). Phases: I (1st preparation) about months 1-4, II (1st competition) about month 5, III (2nd preparation) about months 6-8, IV (2nd competition) about months 9-11. The phase boundaries and dashed lines do not fall exactly on the month ticks (phase I ends late in month 4; phase III ends during month 8). Block 1 is a tall shaded rectangle over about months 1-3, ending late in month 3. Block 2 is a shorter rectangle over about months 6-7: it starts at the month 5/6 tick and ends just past the month 7/8 tick, early in month 8. It is roughly two thirds of block 1's height, matching the text's "smaller volume." Upper panel: the two upper curves bump at about month 1; all three strength curves are lowest at about month 2 and are already rising in month 3, while block 1 is still running. They peak at about month 5, just inside phase II (the two lower curves just right of the first dashed line; the top curve is nearly flat across most of phase II). They dip again during block 2 (lowest about months 6-7), then climb through phase IV to their highest values at month 11. The two upper curves cross just after the phase III/IV line, at about the month 8/9 tick, so only the right-edge order is certain: Starting Strength ends highest, then Explosive Strength, then Maximum Strength. Inference (following each curve smoothly through the crossing): the curve that ends at Starting Strength is the lower of the two upper curves through months 1-8. Lower panel: Technique rises inside block 1, peaks at about month 4 (just after block 1), falls through phase II to a low early in block 2 (about month 6), rises through the rest of block 2 to about its first-peak level by the block's end, peaks at about month 10 and declines toward month 11 (its course through the crossings in months 4-7 is read by continuity). GPP ends above Speed at the right edge (labels). In phase IV the two can be followed: the curve ending at Speed peaks at about months 8-9 and then falls, the curve ending at GPP is lowest at about months 8-9 and then rises, and they cross at about month 10. Before month 8 their courses cross several times and are unclear; the text is the source for GPP being highest in the competitive periods.

**Why it works** — The authors' reason is the LDTE: the concentrated block lowers the athlete's state, and the gain appears afterward, so technique and speed work is timed for the period after the block. For concentrated loading in general they state a mechanism at PDF p. 381 / printed p. 370 (checked against the page image): it "produces a brief, fairly stable state of incomplete restoration which is associated with the persistent and relatively prolonged disturbance of homeostasis. This triggers extensive functional changes which are prerequisites for subsequent supercompensation." The second block can be smaller because it runs "against a background of the adaptation occurring in the first mesocycle" (PDF p. 394). No data are shown for this model; Fig 6.39 is a schematic credited to Siff & Verkhoshansky (1999).

**When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.

-**When NOT to apply** — **Contested by Issurin.** Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that Issurin judged the evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6), and saw the model as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality (p. 11); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. American football is a team sport. Other limits: the model is drawn for "highly qualified athletes" (the concentrated method "was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes," PDF p. 381); the block rectangles are not literal ("The use of rectangular blocks should not create the impression that the concentrated loads are applied suddenly at peak intensity," PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380); and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar (PDF p. 391). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: that rule fits the model's phase IV, where the strength block is over, but the model gives no in-season strength dose, and the baseline's game week ("lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game," line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)) is a microcycle rule the annual model does not address.

+**When NOT to apply** — **Contested, on two grounds that need to be kept apart.** (1) *The annual structure, inside the model's own domain (the basis for the `contested` rating).* Issurin's Block Periodization builds the year from training stages that "should be about two months," four to seven a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], Block Periodization PDF pp. 38-40), and reports world-class track and field athletes, jumpers among them, peaking 7 to 11 times in a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]]). That is a different structure from this model's two large mesocycles; see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]]. (2) *Issurin 2016 on the concentrated block, which bears on transferring the model to football, not on the model in its own domain.* Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that the concentrated-unidirectional model "was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities" (brief, p. 11). It also records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that the author judged that evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. The brief does not name jumping or throwing as narrow-target sports, and it does not reject the model for them. Inference: a single explosive event is the clearest case of "a narrow target quality," so the brief does not count against this model where the authors place it; it counts against transferring it to American football, a team sport whose performance rests on many interacting abilities, and for team sports the reviewed studies reported no effect on practice or competitive performance. The brief also says the review's study selection is non-systematic and author-curated, so this is the reviewer's judgment, not pooled evidence. Other limits: the model is drawn for "highly qualified athletes" (the concentrated method "was devised for preparing highly qualified athletes," PDF p. 381); the block rectangles are not literal ("The use of rectangular blocks should not create the impression that the concentrated loads are applied suddenly at peak intensity," PDF p. 391 / printed p. 380); and stage boundaries "can vary somewhat" with the real calendar (PDF p. 391). Eric's baseline: "In-season, the stated rule is "maintain intensity, reduce volume" rather than trying to build strength while managing a full competition schedule" (line 105, Inferred (transcript + shared slides); the baseline adds "Not claimed in the interview"). Inference: that rule fits the model's phase IV, where the strength block is over, but the model gives no in-season strength dose, and the baseline's game week ("lifting and hard practice end 72 hours before a Saturday game," line 186, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q15)) is a microcycle rule the annual model does not address.

**Example** — The authors give the model, not a worked year (Fig 6.39, PDF p. 395). Inference: for a jumper with indoor and outdoor seasons, block 1 would sit in the first three months of autumn preparation with the jumps, weights and depth-jump sequence inside it, the indoor season would fall about month 5, block 2 would run about months 6-7 at less volume and more intensity, and the main outdoor competitions would fall in months 9-11.

lines: **What it is** — The authors define the two ways of organising training: "Complex loading involves prescription of multi-faceted training regimes to achieve several different fitness objectives over the same period, whereas the concentrated loading method concentrates for a given period on producing a single major specific fitness quality via the use of a unidirectional regime of training" (PDF p. 379 / printed p. 368). "For instance, a complex workout might comprise resistance training, plyometrics and sprinting; a complex microcycle (typically a week) might employ those same training means on different days or during different sessions on the same day." Their case against complex training for top athletes (PDF pp. 380-381 / printed pp. 369-370, all pages checked against the images):

See [[claim--prolonged-competition-period-volume-cuts-lower-special-work-capacity]].

- "Within a monocycle of periodisation, it provides a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training": "The first block contains general conditioning strength work, while the second block emphasizes the development of local muscular endurance," carrying work capacity "right up to the important competitions in the 10th and 11th months" (PDF p. 396).

- Fig 6.41, read by eye: phase I about months 1-6, phase II about months 6-11; block 1 over about months 2-3, block 2 over about months 6-7. Aerobic capacity peaks around the start of the competition period and then eases, as the text says ("maximum aerobic productivity at the beginning of the competition period, and some decrease," PDF p. 397).

**When to apply** — Annual planning for middle-distance (medium) or long-distance (long) endurance athletes who use strength blocks. Not a football model; the medium-duration sequence "General endurance > Speed > Speed-endurance" is the transferable idea. Eric's baseline: "A sport cannot maximize all three energy systems at once" and "priority has to be picked based on what the competition actually demands" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 115, Explicit; the two phrases are joined by a dash in the baseline). Inference: both models pick one energy-system emphasis per stage in that spirit.

-**When NOT to apply** — Long-duration sports are given a monocycle, while the 6.13 aims call for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389); see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]] for this internal conflict. The models are for qualified athletes and carry the same Issurin 2016 challenge to concentrated loading as the other 6.14 models ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Fig 6.46's caption says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading," but the figure prints "GPP" under A and "Strength Load" under B; which wave is the strength block is unclear.

+**When NOT to apply** — Long-duration sports are given a monocycle, while the 6.13 aims call for "at least two large mesocycles... even in sports which traditionally... use monocyclic periodisation" (PDF p. 389); the monocycle here still provides "a two-stage organisation of strength and speed training" (PDF p. 396), and [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]] reads the two passages as a terminology tension (number of mesocycles versus number of competition peaks), not opposed positions. The models are for qualified athletes and carry the same Issurin 2016 challenge to concentrated loading as the other 6.14 models ([[framework--bi-cyclic-annual-model-for-explosive-strength-sports]]). Fig 6.46's caption says "A is the block of concentrated strength loading," but the figure prints "GPP" under A and "Strength Load" under B; which wave is the strength block is unclear.

**Example** — The authors give the schematics only. Inference: an 800 m runner competes at 400 m and 1500 m in the first competition stage as control tests, then runs the main 800 m season in months 10-11 after a smaller second block focused on local muscular endurance.

**When NOT to apply** — The authors themselves warn that the body is non-linear and deviates "fairly random[ly]" from quantitative prediction, so a model is a guide, not a forecast. Their example norms (Tables 6.6-6.12) come from Soviet track-and-field and weightlifting populations of the 1970s and 1980s and are "not... all-embracing models" (PDF p. 391; the sentence is printed with a double negative, "None of these examples should not be regarded as all-embracing models"). No football descriptive model is given.

-**Example** — The authors' own examples are the model-characteristic tables, including weightlifters' muscle and fat proportions and PWC170 by weight class (Table 6.6, Stepanova et al, 1983, PDF p. 391) and 100 m sprinter models ([[case-study--tabachnik-100m-sprinter-model-characteristics]]).

+**Example** — The authors' own examples are the model-characteristic tables, including weightlifters' muscle and fat proportions and PWC170 by weight class (Table 6.6, Stepanova et al, 1983, PDF p. 391) and 100 m sprinter models ([[case-study--tabachnik-100m-sprinter-model-characteristics]]). The other tables on PDF pp. 392-393 / printed pp. 381-382, read from the page images:

+- **Middle distance (Table 6.7, Classes III to I; Table 6.10, CMS and MS 800 m and 1500 m runners; Maximenko, 1979).** Flexibility counts as a model characteristic: "Stride splits (degrees)" and "Straddle splits (degrees)" (for example, stride splits of 111.5, 116.8 and 131.5 degrees for Classes III, II and I). Special endurance has a defined test, "2 series of 4 x 400m, with 2 mins rest between each 400m and 8-10 mins rest between each series" (Table 6.7 caption). The strength row is printed "Relative mean strength of 5 muscle groups (kg)," while the caption describes "the mean of the strength of the extensors and flexors of the hip, knee and ankle joints relative to bodymass"; the unit and the muscle-group count are recorded as printed.

+- **Javelin (Table 6.11, Konstantinov, 1978), international-class throwers, men / women.** Snatch "Bmass + 15kg" / "Bmass+10kg"; back squat "2 x Bmass" / "1.5 x Bmass"; standing broad jump 3.20 / 2.80 m; standing triple jump 10.20 / 7.80 m; vertical jump 95.0 / 70.0 cm; 30 m from a running start 2.90 / 3.20 s; throws of assistance objects or the javelin "with average intensity" 170 / 140 times and javelin throws "with above average intensity" 35 / 30 times (the table gives no time period for these counts). Inference: this is the chapter's closest thing to a strength and power norm table for a power athlete.

+- **Juvenile sprinters (Table 6.12, Alabin & Yushkevitch, 1978), ages 11-16.** The row "Standing quintuple jump (cm)" prints 9.25 at age 11 rising to 13.70 at age 16. Inference: the values must be metres; a quintuple jump of 9-14 cm is impossible, and the standing long jump row of the same table runs 179.8-261.2 cm.

## Figure readings (my own, from the renders)

**Fig 6.39 (PDF 395), months "about".** Month numerals sit between tick marks; dashed lines at late month 4 (I/II), the month 5/6 tick (II/III), mid month 8 (III/IV). Block 1: start to late month 3. Block 2: month 5/6 tick to just past the month 7/8 tick, about two thirds of block 1's height.
- Upper panel. The top two curves bump early in month 1. All three are lowest at about month 2 (Maximum Strength slightly earlier), and they are rising through month 3 inside block 1. Peaks: Maximum Strength and the middle curve just right of the I/II dashed line (early month 5); the top curve is a flat top across phase II. Lows in block 2 at about months 6-7. Highest at month 11. The two upper curves cross just right of the III/IV line, at about the month 8/9 tick. By smooth continuation the steeply rising lower curve becomes the top one, so Starting Strength is the lower of the two through months 1-8 (Inference). Right-edge order: Starting, Explosive, Maximum (certain).
- Lower panel. Technique peaks at about month 4, is lowest at about month 6 (early block 2), and is back to about its first-peak level at block 2's end. That is level with the first peak, not clearly above it as the review says. It peaks at about month 10 and declines toward month 11. In phase IV: the Speed curve peaks at about months 8-9 and falls, the GPP curve is lowest at about months 8-9 and rises, and they cross at about month 10. Before month 8, GPP and Speed are unclear.
- Agreement with the review: (1), (3), (4) and the right-edge order hold. On (2), the peaks are at the very start of phase II (about early month 5), consistent with the review's "inside phase II, just after the first dashed line"; the old "months 4-5 (around the phase I/II boundary)" was close but placed them on the boundary.

**Fig 6.32(b) (PDF 383).** Two curves above the axis leave the origin inside the block. One rises steadily, concave up, to S-E. The other peaks about 70% of the way through the block, falls to a low after it, rises to a second hump and eases, ending at An-Gly. Two curves dip below the axis (one deeper) and cross back above it after the block, ending at Vmax and STATE; which one ends where is unclear. One curve starts at the block's right edge and rises steeply to a mid-panel peak, then falls to Speed. The S-E and Vmax identities depend on continuity through crossings at about two thirds of the panel width (Inference).

**Fig 6.36(b) (PDF 388).**
- Aerobic week: VO2 max starts about 87%, crosses 100% at about 35 h, about 107% at 72 h. Training effect starts about 93%, crosses at about 15-18 h, about 101.5-102% at 72 h.
- Anaerobic week: VO2 max starts just under 100%, peaks about 113% at about 6-10 h, about 106% at 72 h. Training effect starts about 94%, crosses at about 38-40 h, about 102.5-103% at 72 h.
- The review's "about 30-36 h" for both crossings is close for the aerobic panel but early for the anaerobic one.

lines: **When to apply** — Planning a year for an explosive-strength sport with two clearly separated competition phases: put the large strength block early in the first preparation phase, a smaller and more intense block early in the second preparation phase, keep technique work going at reduced intensity inside each block, and shift to technique, speed and competition readiness as the delayed effect appears. Eric's baseline: "In football the target is a peak every Saturday, with November and the postseason as the priority window" (`docs/method-baseline.md`, line 185, Explicit (interview 2026-09-28, Q14)). Inference: football has one long competition phase, not two, so the model maps onto the football year only partly: a large block in the winter off-season and a smaller, more intense block in the summer before fall camp would follow the model's block sizes, with phase IV standing in for the season. The authors do not discuss football or weekly competition.

-**When NOT to apply** — **Contested, on two grounds that need to be kept apart.** (1) *The annual structure, inside the model's own domain (the basis for the `contested` rating).* Issurin's Block Periodization builds the year from training stages that "should be about two months," four to seven a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/framework--training-stage-and-multi-peak-annual-cycle]], Block Periodization PDF pp. 38-40), and reports world-class track and field athletes, jumpers among them, peaking 7 to 11 times in a season ([[block-periodization--issurin/claim--multi-peak-annual-preparation-elite-track-and-field]]). That is a different structure from this model's two large mesocycles; see [[claim--two-large-mesocycles-a-year-bi-cyclic-organisation]]. (2) *Issurin 2016 on the concentrated block, which bears on transferring the model to football, not on the model in its own domain.* Every model in 6.14 uses the concentrated block: "All models in this chapter use the principle of concentrated special strength loading, which elicits the LDTE" (PDF p. 390 / printed p. 379, checked against the page image). The library's brief of Issurin 2016 records that the concentrated-unidirectional model "was presented as better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality and as restricted when peak performance requires many interacting abilities" (brief, p. 11). It also records that concentrated-unidirectional programs in combat and team sports "improved some fitness measures, but the reviewed studies did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance," and that the author judged that evidence "insufficient for broad implementation in high-performance combat, team-sport, and swimming preparation" (brief, p. 6); see [[research-papers/issurin-2016-benefits-and-limitations-of-block-periodized-training-approaches-to-athletes-preparation-a]]. The brief does not name jumping or throwing as narrow-target sports, and it does not reject the model for them. Inference: a single explosive event is the clearest case of "a narrow target quality," so the brief does not count against this model where the authors place it; it counts against transferring it to American football, a team sport whose performance rests on many interacting abilities, and for team sports the reviewed studies reported no effect on practice or competitive performance. The brief also says the review's study selection is non-systematic and author-curated, so this is Issurin's judgment, not pooled evidence. I applied all 11 fixes to the 6d entries and none are left open; I disagreed with the review's wording or numbers in 7 places, recorded in the log. The 6d files have no lint lines, the grep proof shows every fix landed, and none of the old wording remains.

The log is at `/Users/kristinarash/DEV/Flint/staging/fixes_supertraining_ch6d_applied.md`. The scope file is unchanged at 25 lines, nothing was renamed, and I made no edits to 6b, 6c, `_book.md` or the vault. None of the 25 files cites the Addendum (0 matches across 25 files), so no attribution change was needed.

## Per-fix outcome
| # | Entry | Outcome |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | explosive-strength bi-cyclic model | Applied. Fig 6.39 rewritten from my own reading. The Issurin 2016 challenge now quotes the brief exactly and is scoped to the football transfer. Stays `contested`, on a different basis than the review gave (see below). |
| 2 | tri-cyclic | Applied. The boxing/swimming citation is corrected; moved from `supported` to `contested`. |
| 3 | two mesocycles | Applied. The "internal conflict" is now a terminology tension (PDF 387 against 389 and 396); `contested` rests on Issurin. |
| 4 | complex training | Applied. Issurin agrees with the critique and contests the remedy and the beginners limit. Added the brief's caveat that the 28 studies are Issurin's own selection. Matveyev 1970 is now its own clause. |
| 5 | speed sport, Fig 6.32(b) | Applied, with one change: An-Gly peaks late in the block, not mid-block. |
| 6 | microcycles | Applied. The false 12 h conflict is removed and I used my own crossing times. Missing idea 4 is added here. |
| 7 | Tabachnik | Applied. Added the 5 m (1.18 s) against 15 m (1.16-1.18 s) inconsistency and the review's optional point on the 15 m step. |
| 8 | loading reduction | Applied. PDF 305's 1-3 week latency now sits beside "far longer than 1-2 weeks"; added the link to rule 2 of the 6c time-technique entry. |
| 9 | Antonova/Levchenko | Applied, plus one extra: PDF 381 also dates Antonova 1980 (1982 elsewhere). Added the 6c LDTE link. |
| 10 | prolonged competition | Applied ("comparable", not "shorter"). |
| 11 | follow-a-concentrated-block | Applied. The text supports the figure labels, so the caption is the likelier error (marked Inference). |

**Where I disagreed with the review (all in the log):**
- **The two review rows apply different rules.** One keeps the explosive model `contested` for football only; the other says a contest should follow the entry's own sport domain. I applied the domain rule to all four Issurin-related entries.
- **"Jumping-type sports" is not in the brief.** Your prompt and the review both paraphrase p. 11 that way. The brief says only "better suited to sports dominated by a narrow target quality". The entry quotes that and says the brief names no jumping or throwing sports; the link to explosive events is marked Inference.
- **Fig 6.39 Technique** ends block 2 about level with its first peak, not above it.
- **Fig 6.36(b) crossings** are about 35 h and 38-40 h, not 30-36 h.
- **The brief's "repeats the book's critique"** refers to Issurin's own book, not Supertraining, so the entry says so.
- **Antonova's dates** also slip (1980 at PDF 381), which the review did not list.

## Figure readings (all values "about")
- **Fig 6.39** (400 dpi crops):
  - Block 1 runs from the start to late month 3. Block 2 runs from the month 5/6 tick to just past the month 7/8 tick, about two thirds of block 1's height.
  - Strength curves: the top two bump in month 1. All three are lowest at month 2 and already rising in month 3, while block 1 is still running. They peak in early month 5, just inside phase II, dip in months 6-7 and are highest at month 11.
  - The two upper curves cross at the month 8/9 tick. Right-edge order Starting, Explosive, Maximum is certain; which curve is which before the crossing is Inference.
  - Technique peaks at month 4, is lowest at month 6, is back to its first-peak level by the end of block 2, peaks at month 10 and declines.
  - GPP and Speed can only be told apart in phase IV: Speed peaks at months 8-9 and falls, GPP is lowest there and rises, and they cross at month 10. Before month 8 they are unclear.
- **Fig 6.32(b)** (400 and 600 dpi):
  - Two curves dip below the axis during the block and end at Vmax and STATE; which is which is unclear.
  - S-E rises steadily.
  - An-Gly peaks about 70% of the way through the block, falls, then rises to a second hump.
  - Speed starts only at the block's end.
- **Fig 6.36(b)** (400 dpi):
  - Aerobic week: VO2 max goes from 87% to 100% at 35 h and 107% at 72 h. Training effect goes from 93% to 100% at 15-18 h.
  - Anaerobic week: VO2 max peaks at 113% around 6-10 h and falls to 106%. Training effect goes from 94% to 100% at 38-40 h and 102.5-103% at 72 h.

## Confidence for the four Issurin-related entries
The test for all four: does a library source disagree with the entry inside the sport domain the entry claims?
- **Explosive model: `contested`.** Issurin's 2008 book disputes the two-mesocycle structure in this domain: stages of about two months, four to seven a season, and world-class jumpers peaking 7-11 times a season. Issurin 2016 does not count against the model in its own domain. It counts against transferring it to football, a team sport (brief p. 6: studies "did not report effects on team practice or competitive performance").
- **Tri-cyclic: `contested` (was `supported`).** Brief p. 6 names combat sports and swimming, which are inside this model's stated domain, and the model runs on concentrated blocks.
- **Two mesocycles: `contested`.** Rests on Issurin's 2008 book. The entry says the 2016 brief does not address mesocycle count.
- **Complex training: `contested`.** Issurin contests the remedy (a minimal number of targets per block, not one) and the beginners limit (brief p. 11, amateurs). The 28 studies are his own non-systematic selection.

## Missing ideas
- **1-3** (Table 6.11 javelin norms, Tables 6.7/6.10 middle distance, and the Table 6.12 "Standing quintuple jump (cm)" values of 9.25-13.70, marked as Inference that they must be metres): added to `framework--descriptive-and-prescriptive-training-models`.
- **4** (PDF 387 "currently scant" findings): added to the microcycle case study, with the reason it stays `supported`.
- **5** (PDF 396 "deferred"): added to the endurance entry.

No new entry was needed.
